speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, February 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-139, to amend the statute law relating to Income Tax (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker, a recent poll indicated that the general public is becoming more and more convinced that the present Government has neither the ability nor the will to address effectively the basic problems threatening our economy. The several attempts made by the Government to produce a budget that would deal with our problems have proved to be abject disasters. Rather than bringing new hope and confidence to Canadians, what the Government has done has resulted in ever-deepening frustration and fear.
In November, 1981 the Government introduced one of the most complex and controversial budgets in Canadian history. Even the Government itself was disgusted with it. No less than 162 income tax changes and 56 changes in other tax related statutes were proposed. Subsequent budgets in June and October, 1982 altered parts of the November budget and proposed new measures.
Bill C-139 was not introduced until December 7, 1982, more than a full year after the November, 1981 budget. In December, 1982 it received a one-day debate. In January, 1983 Bill C-139 was debated for one-half day. In spite of the proclaimed importance of the measures contained in Bill C-139, the Government decided to debate Bills to reduce the indexing of Public Service pensions, Family Allowance benefits and Old Age Security pensions. Then to make things even worse the Government brought in the Canagrex Bill for debate.
The Government now insists that Bill C-139 be passed with dispatch because it claims that no income tax refunds can be paid until it has been passed. If this is true, why has the Government insisted on dealing with the other measures to which I have alluded instead of dealing with Bill C-139? Perhaps the Ministry and officials have been as confused and uncertain of the ramifications of the measures proposed as has the general public. Perhaps the Government and the Minister were not prepared to explain those ramifications. Could it be
that the Government delayed it, as it did, so the Government could use the guillotine once again to silence the Opposition? If this Bill must be passed before refunds are paid, how could the Government reduce Family Allowances before the legislation was passed?
There is another question. Why has the Government used other means to delay the issuing of refunds? Interest on refunds is not paid until after April 30, nor is it paid between the date that the refund is processed and the date that it is received and cashed by the taxpayer. Yet another question is, why were tax forms mailed out a month later than usual? Many taxpayers were forced to have special forms not hitherto required, further delaying their file.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) stated that early passage of the legislation will help Revenue Canada get on with the job of processing the 1982 returns. He concluded; "I therefore look forward to a speedy debate".
Bill C-139 is 300 pages thick. This House is urged to give it speedy passage after long months of hesitation, delay and confusion on the part of the Government. Bill C-139 will increase the tax burden on many Canadians through its increased taxation of employee benefits, its measures with respect to the income averaging, accrued interest income, the abolition of general averaging provisions and others. Many other taxpayers will be seriously affected by provisions that remove incentives under the guise of closing loopholes. In other words, the Government is so determined to extract every penny possible from the taxpayer that anything goes.
The former Minister of Finance pronounced that the budget was based on equity, justice and renewal. In actual fact, it fails all three tests and many of the tax measures in Bill C-139 are inequitable, unjust and oppressive.
I believe that action is required in several different areas. First, tax laws should be made understandable for the ordinary Canadian, including myself. Presently, no one seems to know, understand or be able to determine the jargon of the Income Tax Act. Second, there is the need to recognize the rights of Canadians to manage their own affairs rather than having the state confiscate the bulk of their income, leaving them only a little pocket money. Third, a review of the tax structure is essential to ensure equity and justice for all. I think back through the years to the many times that we were told there would be a review of the tax structure. Unfortunately, that review always seems to result in higher taxes. I suggest that is not good enough for the people at this time.

March 1, 1983
Income Tax
Time is needed to examine this Bill carefully in order to approve what is good, acceptable and equitable and to delete what is contrary to the best interests of Canada and Canadians. Therefore, I suggest there should be ample time made available to give thorough study to this entire tax Bill and, due to its complexity, it will take a considerable length of time to complete the review and to bring in the changes that will be necessary in order to give justice to the Canadian people.
I appreciate the opportunity to take part in this debate today. Certainly, as the day progresses, I am sure that many other proposals will be made that will further delete the unacceptable portions of the Bill and make it more acceptable to the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to associate myself wholeheartedly with the remarks of the distinguished Member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Patterson), who is one of the more senior Members of the House.
I cannot think of any Bill, nor do I believe the Hon. Member, considering his long history in the House, could think of a Bill other than the one presently under discussion, Bill C-139, which more graphically represents the mess created by the Government in this country. This is evident in the provisions contained in this massive and almost incomprehensible tax Bill. Never has the Parliament of Canada been so insulted by having to attend to consider, in a comprehensible way, a tax measure which, in effect, amounts to two budgets with three amending financial statements.
I will not refer to all of the budgets because there have been so many. The former Minister of Finance presented a budget in November of 1981, an amendment in December of 1981, and his second real budget in June of 1982. Then the financial statements of the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) were announced in October of 1982 and his latest statement was heard just the other day. However, all of their predictions as to estimates of revenues and expenditures have been wrong.
As the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley East mentioned, this legislation comes down to a Bill comprising 297 pages, introduced in the House as late as December 7, 1982, taking approximately 380 days for the officials even to write the Bill. Then just before the Christmas recess and after we came back, the Minister of Finance had the temerity and the gall to suggest that Members of Parliament should sweep all these problems aside, without proper understanding of what is involved.
I will point out the many provisions in the Bill in general because there is not enough time in the ten minutes allotted to me under our present rules to go into them in detail. Because Hon. Members are restricted to ten minutes, it is impossible to discuss the Bill meaningfully, even in general. However, to return to the subject, the Government, in its fifteenth year, having come to power in 1968 with a budget of some $10 billion, is now estimating a budget of $90 billion, with a deficit projected by the Minister of Finance of almost $30 billion
before the fiscal year is over. This sum is more than the total budgets-not deficits-of all the Provinces except Ontario and Quebec. In fact, half of their budgets could be added and it would still not amount to $30 billion.
Hon. Members are confronted with this Bill, which is to produce revenue, in the face of the billions of dollars which have been wrongly estimated. It is no wonder that many people in and out of this House are saying that the situation is incomprehensible and must be changed.
In a speech last week in Ottawa, J. Lyman Maclnnis, the senior partner of Touche, Ross and Company, President of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Ontario, said: "The Canadian Income Tax Act is an unmitigated mess". Then he said: "I started out by saying that income tax is an unmitigated mess. The reason I say that is because it is incomprehensible".
I am prepared to agree with him and would venture a guess that only the minority of a minority in the House, not the majority but, rather, those who are really involved in the study of tax law, can even begin to understand the smorgasbord of legislation contained in the Bill which will smother Canadians in increased taxes, not to mention the red tape involved in figuring them out.
There are 24 items covered in the Bill as follows: auto standby charges; life insurance and annuities; Small Business Bonds; soft costs; RRSP interest deductibility; IAACs; work-in-progress; capital gain reserves; metric measures; principal residence provisions; retiring allowance provisions; housing loans; six and five re. tax indexation; forward averaging; small business lower tax limit and loss of cumulative dividend account; corporate surtax; iron ore processing; DPSPs; 12.5 per cent small business distributions tax; 5 per cent reduction on withholding tax rescinded; director's liability; confidentiality; charitable foundations; capital cost allowance reduction.
Another item which is not specifically listed is the fuel compensation tax which would put Canadian shippers and the aviation industry at a disadvantage when competing with our American brothers or neighbours. This tax has to be removed before this Bill can proceed.
Many years ago the then Minister of Transport said one of the most profound things ever said in this House when talking about transportation. He said: "Transport is in a mess". That was not said by the present Minister but by one of his illustrious predecessors. That Minister of Transport was right because transportation was in a mess. Unfortunately, it is still in a mess.
What is in even more of a mess is the income tax provisions which are assaulting and insulting Canadians from coast to coast. We have very little time, Mr. Speaker, to really discuss some of the provisions of this Bill which I have mentioned. I should mention one basic and fundamental thing about these provisions. They provide no incentive to Canadians. They
March 1, 1983

provide no incentive for individual Canadians to participate in the development of the fundamental resources of this land.
At this stage of our parliamentary life I suggest that Members cannot really understand or comprehend the provisions this income tax Bill comprising 297 pages and incorporating two budgets and three financial statements by two Ministers of Finance. I do not think anyone really knows what the implications of this Bill are, not even the tax people, I suggest. Incidentally, it took some 300 days to write this Bill.
I was trying to think of something even more profound to say about this Bill than the fact that it is completely incomprehensible even to the chartered accountants across this land, those chartered accountants who are very careful people. The President of the Chartered Accountants Association was defining what he meant by the Bill being incomprehensible when he said that it runs completely contrary to three fundamental tax legislation measures, the first being that it has to be clear so that taxpayers can understand it.
Taxpayers are the people who assess their own taxes, and if they do not understand the wording-and the average taxpayer cannot understand the wording of this Bill-they cannot intelligently file tax returns. When the individual taxpayer does not understand the wording of tax legislation, or even the income tax return, he does not have a reasonable chance of filing an accurate return. The average Canadian is not in a position to hire a professional for assistance because the cost of hiring that professional is not deductible. The wording of this Bill falls completely short of that fundamental principle.
The President of the Association of Chartered Accountants has suggested that there should be holding legislation while we digest the tax laws which now exist. Quite frankly, I would like to discuss some of the tax laws we now have, but I do not have the time to do so at this stage.
In conclusion, I want to leave the House with this one basic thought which illustrates the mess the Government of Canada has made of the economy of this land. If the Government cannot look after its own business, let alone its tax laws, no wonder there is such a mess and such confusion in Canada. How many Members of this House can tell me today when this session of Parliament started? I would bet not too many Members can tell me. I would bet that the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Smith) could not tell me the date on which this Parliament started. We are in our 465th day of this Parliament which started on April 14, 1980. The Hon. Member got some help from someone behind the curtains there, and 1 suggest this is the first time there has been an intelligent comment from behind the curtains over on that side. The length of this Parliament is an insult to Members of Parliament and Canadian taxpayers. This Parliament has been meandering along for 465 days, starting three years ago on April 14, 1980.
1 want to read a little bit of the history of another long Parliament, a long session of the Parliament in England which took place many years ago. Let me quote from "An Encyclopaedia of Parliament", written by co-authors, one of whom
Income Tax
is presently one of our distinguished Table officers, Philip Laundy, who collaborated with Norman Wilding in the writing of this most interesting encyclopaedia of the British Parliament. At page 438 the following is stated:
The fifth and last Parliament to be summoned by Charles I. It met on 3 November 1640, and in 1642 it took up arms against the King.
I could make a speech about what we should do in that vein around here. The paragraph continues as follows:
It is possibly the most historic assembly ever to have sat at Westminster, and it was said of it that many thought it would never have a beginning, and afterwards that it would never have an end.
During its long life, which extended over twenty years, it underwent many changes. In 1648 it was purged of those members who were too favourable to the King;-
Listen to this, Mr. Speaker. 1 am almost through.
-in 1649 it abolished both the Monarchy and the House of Lords;-
We are not sure what will happen in this country.
-it was expelled by Cromwell in 1653; recalled and expelled again in 1659; restored for the last time, with its excluded members later recalled at the end of that year; and finally dissolved on 16 March 1660.
These are the closing two sentences:
It commenced its long existence as a formidable and enthusiastic assembly, bent upon drastic reform, the champion of the liberties of the people against the tyranny of the King. It sank eventually into corruption, ignominy, and discredit, having subverted the Constitution it had set out to uphold, and having lost many of its greatest members through death or exclusion.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking to Bill C-139 1 hope you will give me the latitude to dwell on certain aspects of the fiscal regime of the Government because they are all interrelated.
In addressing myself to this Bill, I am reminded of the words of an unknown author who said:
Tell me today what the philosopher thinks, the university professor expounds, the schoolmaster teaches, the scholar publishes in his treatises and textbooks and I shall prophesy the conduct of individuals, the ethics of businessmen, the schemes of political leaders, the plans of economists, the pleading of lawyers, the decisions of judges, the legislation of lawmakers, the treaties of diplomats and the decisions of state a generation hence.
The author of this wisdom is unknown but history bears him out. The foundations of the present Canadian economic crisis were well laid in the sixties and the seventies. What we do economically and politically today will lay the foundations for the latter half of the eighties and the nineties and, indeed, well into the next century.
Like so many other Canadians, I am concerned about three characteristics of the foundations we are now laying in our nation. They are as follows: First, the growth and awesome complexity of the system of laws that govern our Canadian society; second, the growth of governments at all levels in this nation; third, the accumulation of public debt.

March 1, 1983
Income Tax
In Canada the economic distemper of the sixties and seventies has created the instability of the eighties. Our problem is a lack of productivity. We have in the past traded the pride of doing for the enjoyment of loafing. We have bound ourselves with a system of laws so complex and pervasive that initiative, entrepreneurship and collective productivity is stifled.
A very good friend of mine who is the president of a very large Canadian corporation recently told me that we as a society support a system of complex laws in every area of endeavour and particularly in the financial, business and property exchange areas of taxation. Why, he said, there are approximately 40,000 lawyers in Canada and only approximately 15,000 research scientists. 1 looked up the actual figures. There are 40,043 lawyers in Canada and 15,270 research scientists. In the United States there are 320,000 lawyers and 828,000 research scientists. Lawyers produce no goods and little real wealth but lots of paper. They often retard the production of wealth and establish massive, complex and intricate systems for wealth redistribution. He said we need three times as many research scientists and only half as many lawyers.
This Income Tax Act, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-139 now before this House, is an example of the complexity of the legal system under which we have to perform. This Bill is an abomination. Its 295 pages of incomprehensible gobbledygook are designed to throttle and subdue industrial and personal initiative. What greater example is there of an overly complex law than Bill C-139, the Income Tax Act, literally 295 pages of legal shackling? The Government would be very wise to lay before the Law Reform Commission of Canada a new mandate to simplify the network of laws governing the entire business sector of this country.
The capital gains tax structure must surely be dismantled immediately before it further legally imprisons all who dare to do business or own property in this land. The capital gains taxation scheme will lay upon this nation a system requiring bookkeeping and interpretation of enormous complexity and will stifle business at every opportunity.
Canada and the free world have so concentrated on the public process of wealth redistribution in the last several decades that we have lost sight of the process of wealth production. Even though scientific discoveries have given us enormous capability to produce wealth, the process of public redistribution of this wealth has indeed laid upon the production systems of the free world some terrible "disincentives". My very first speech in this House in 1979, Mr. Speaker, was concerned with the abnormal growth of governments in the free world, including Canada. Taxation to take away the productivity of the people and recycle it through the public process of distribution has gotten out of hand. Governments at all levels grew like mushrooms regardless of their political persuasions.
Canada is a prime example of this growth on all three levels. I do not mind admitting that I was a Member of the Progressive Conservative Government in a Province in which the budget increased by nine times in less than a decade. Indeed,
the Saturday edition of The Globe and Mail of February 19 has a chart showing the growth of governments in Canada as a percentage of the GNP. Since 1964, a mere 18 years ago, provincial and municipal governments have grown from about 16 per cent of the GNP to approximately 28.5 per cent of the GNP. So it is not only the federal Government which has grown like a mushroom. The federal Government has jumped from about 13 per cent of the GNP to 21 per cent in 18 years.
In 1983 the growth of Government is explosive and scary. Indeed, during the current fiscal year, the total expenditures of all three levels of Government are expected to reach almost 50 per cent of the GNP. Part of it, of course, is in connection with Bill C-139. In other words, Mr. Speaker, in Canada this current year the Government will take for redistribution $1 of every $2 earned in the private sector. I believe this will give rise to an unstable situation and a continuing and deepening recession coupled with increasing inflation.
It is unfortunate, Mr. Speaker, that I have so little time left because I wanted to get into the increasing debt in the provincial and municipal areas as well as in the federal Government, and the awesome load which this increase in debt would lay upon the entrepreneurs in the business sector of Canada in the short term as well as in the long term. Obviously, I do not have time so I thank you for the ten minutes you have given me.

Mr. Speaker, the legislation now being debated by the House of Commons is a mammoth 297-page document designed to implement the far-reaching tax changes brought forward by the federal Government in its infamous budget of November, 1981. From the time that budget was announced in the House by the now Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), there have been so many revisions that one would need to be a computer to keep track of them all, let alone fully understand the implications of the changes involved. But what is clear is this: the November, 1981 budget sought to revamp the entire tax system without a thorough study of what specific reforms were needed, without an understanding of the impact of such fundamental tax changes on the average citizen, and without prior consultation with those affected.
In a nutshell, sir, the then Minister of Finance sought to close so-called tax loopholes in order to make the tax system more equitable and to raise much needed revenue for the federal Treasury. In the process, however, the Minister's tax changes ended up hurting most severely the very Canadians he had naively intended to assist, namely, the low- and middle-income earners. Clearly, the Minister of Finance of the day did not know what he was doing. As a result, both he and his successor had to devote most of their energies in the following months to trying to undo the damage caused by the budget.
To this very day, Mr. Speaker, the Government continues to patch and fill its tax program to the point where even experts are in the dark as to where matters now stand. Indeed, when asked to provide a list of tax changes since November, 1981,
March 1, 1983

the Department of Finance was forced to admit that no such list exists. Unfortunately, despite the countless flip-flops by the Government, some of the most damaging provisions in the Government's program remain. The net effect will be that the average individual taxpayer and the average small business will be hit with substantially higher taxes if Bill C-139 is passed.
While waiting for Parliament to dispose of the legislation, the Government is delaying the processing of tax returns for the past income tax year because many of the provisions in the Bill apply retroactively to 1982 and the Government covets every extra tax penny it can squeeze out of an already overburdened taxpayer. The federal Government's adamant refusal to process income tax returns speedily is nothing less than scandalous.
Millions of Canadians, sir, are desperately waiting for their tax refunds merely to put bread on the table during the current deepening recession. Each year, as you will know, some 15 million Canadians file income tax returns. On average, after all returns are processed, the Government ends up owing about $3 billion more to taxpayers than taxpayers owe to the Government. The many taxpayers who lost their jobs during part of last year will likely be entitled to even larger refunds this year than in previous years. That is because the Government probably deducted too much tax at source on the assumption that those people who were laid off would be employed during the whole year. If such people are still out of work today, as many of them are, they will need their refunds urgently, especially if their Unemployment Insurance has run out or is running out.
Yet the Government says it wants to wait until Bill C-139 is passed by Parliament before issuing refunds. It is also delaying refunds on the ground that Government computers are having to be reprogrammed to reflect recent changes in income tax laws. Mr. Speaker, in a letter to me dated January 7, 1983, Mr. R. W. Mercer, Director of Taxation in the Charlottetown District Office of Revenue Canada, said that full processing of tax returns will not start before March 24, with the first refunds being issued no sooner than mid-May. That is absolutely shocking. By mid-May of last year, about 6.5 million Canadians had already received their income tax refunds. Many had received them as early as March 26. I hear the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) saying to me that the same thing will apply this year. I suggest he go back to his officials and look at the information they are sending out to taxpayers. With hundreds of thousands of Canadians desperately in need of their tax refunds this year just to heat their homes, to put food in their mouths, and to keep the bill collector at bay-as I am trying to keep the Minister of National Revenue at bay while I am speaking-the Government's footdragging concerning tax refunds is a national scandal.
The fact that Parliament has not yet passed the Government's income tax Bill, now before the House, should not be
Income Tax
allowed to stall refunds, just as that fact did not prevent the Government from collecting income tax all along. Nor should the Government get away with blaming computers for the delay. The Government has had 14 months to retool its computers since the tax changes in November, 1981, and it has had at least seven months since those changes were modified in June, 1982. Clearly, the Government is using Bill C-139 and computer retooling-I suggest that the Minister of National Revenue examine the information sent out by his officials-as mere excuses to keep people's tax refunds as long as possible because it is broke and this is an easy way for it to get hold of lots of cash at someone else's expense.
The delay by Revenue Canada in mailing 1982 income tax refunds is forcing large numbers of desperate Canadians to pay exorbitant sums to firms that offer on-the-spot cash for refunds before they are actually received from the Government.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I urge the Government to accelerate the processing of income tax so as to put refund cheques in the hands of Canadians without further delay. In the meantime, the Government should take emergency measures to prevent unscrupulous tax firms from gouging needy taxpayers. The Government should establish mechanisms to process, on a priority basis, the tax returns of Canadians who can establish that they urgently require their refunds because of unemployment or some other factor. And until Bill C-139 becomes law, the Government should tax Canadians on the basis of existing laws, not on the basis of this shoddily drafted and unfair legislation. For the Government to do otherwise would signal that it is more interested in collecting taxes than it is in the welfare of the taxpayers themselves.

Mr. Speaker, the ten minutes allotted to us barely gives time to go into any detail. 1 look forward to this matter coming to Committee of the Whole when Canadians from one end of the country to the other might receive answers to their questions.
I want to deal with two aspects of the Bill. First of all, along with my colleague from Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan) and other Members, I want to express my concern for and fear of the practice being followed by the Government. I still have not received my T-4 slip, Mr. Speaker, and I know that many other Canadians are wondering where theirs are. Usually we have them some time in February. Usually by this time, most Canadians have completed and submitted their income tax returns. Usually by this time, a lot of Canadians have received refunds. That is not the case this year.
The Government has clearly indicated it will not issue income tax refunds for the 1982 tax year until Bill C-139 is passed. That is a form of blackmail. As the Government sees the political process, it may be a useful tool to achieve its ends but it is discriminatory and it is unfair.
Bill C-139 was not introduced until December 7, 1982, more than one year after the November, 1981 budget. Yet the Government asks us to accept its edict, without debate and

March 1, 1983
Income Tax
without argument, that there will be no refunds processed until Bill C-139 is passed.
As the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Patterson) explained earlier today in this Chamber, you cannot trample on or play with casually the lives of Canadians. The Bill before us embraces nearly 200 significant changes. It is so complex as to be barely understandable even to chartered accountants and lawyers. Why the Government chooses to blackmail people, to threaten them, to cause them undue hardship, is beyond me.
The Government obviously wants its money and it is entitled to it. We will not discuss the wastage that has gone on. I say the Government is being unfair and is imposing undue hardship on countless thousands of Canadians by deliberately shutting down the computer system for reprogramming. Who programs in the middle of a program? That is done ahead of time. The Government has deliberately shut down the computer system and it will not start up again until late March or, as the Government says, until Bill C-139 is passed.
The Bill demands a thorough examination by all of us and that examination can follow when the Members have put their views and concerns on record.
1 want to deal with a very specific matter because ten minutes does not allow me enough time to cover the whole bill. I want to deal with the transportation fuel compensation recovery charge that was arbitrarily imposed on the air lines and the marine mode by the Government. It was removed later when the air lines threatened international action but was brought in through the back door by a tax measure in order to recover what had been lost in another process. The marine mode tax is in place; the recovery charge is there. There is no indication from the Government that it has any intention of removing it even on the ground of its being discriminatory. It was removed from the air mode but not from the marine mode. Last year one large shipping company lost 12 voyages because of the fuel tax. That does not include the number of jobs lost to Canadian seamen, officers, marine engineers, shore supply staff, merchantment and suppliers. At a time when we have 1.5 million unemployed, surely it is a piddling amount of money. Probably last year it amounted to 35 per cent to 40 per cent of what they collected in the first year of operation, 1981. There is a direct linkage between the tax and the downturn in activity on the Lakes, yet the Minister persists in this action.
I ask the Minister whether he has appealed to his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). Has he acted as the advocate he should be for the marine industry in the country? Has he made its views known? When we get to Committee of the Whole consideration of this Bill, these will be questions to which we on this side will want direct answers.
We are coming up to another questionable year in respect of the level of activity on the Great Lakes. This tax is discriminatory in the sense that it is imposed on one mode of transportation, not on any others. As we approach the 1983 season,
surely the principal advocate of the marine industry should make known in a very forceful manner the views of the marine industry to the Minister of Finance and other Treasury officials.
This tax is discriminatory. It raises very little money. We understand that approximately $5.5 million was raised in 1981 and that last year, as I said, probably only 35 per cent to 40 per cent of that figure was raised. We are talking about a very small amount of money, yet in the very narrow field of marine transportation it has an enormous and profound impact. We will have some questions about that when we get to Committee of the Whole. We will want to know why we are losing cargoes. We would like to know why the Minister deliberately, obviously and consciously allows this discriminatory tax to remain, especially when we consider its impact. We know what the Dominion Marine Association has said about it. It has consistently requested the removal of this tax on this mode of transportation.
If they go ahead with it in the area of air transportation, either through the front door or the back door, they will create enormous problems for an industry which does not need them and certainly does not deserve them. Seaway tolls are rising. We appeal to the Minister to take a long, hard, new look at increases in Seaway tolls and pilotage fees. Everything is going up and up. The pilotage fees for seasoned river captains of vessels plying coastal waters, the Great Lakes and other harbours are rising. They do not need pilots. Good Lord, in most cases many of these captains and mates are more familiar with the waters they are plying than the pilots they employ and have to pay.
I re-emphasize that this is just a very narrow issue which has a very profound impact on a small sector of Canadian entrepreneurship. It is discriminatory; it should be removed. It will be an issue which we will want the Minister to address himself to when we get to the point in time that we are dealing with the Bill clause by clause in Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker, thank you very much for allowing me this ten minutes to debate Bill C-139, a 295-page tax Bill, full of amendments to one of the most complicated tax Acts the world has ever seen. Government Members opposite are anxious that we seem to be taking time. Of course we are taking time. All they have done and accomplished in their decade of rule over what was once a free country, that once had a private sector of which we were proud and once was able through a good, solid-

Mr. Speaker, I opened my remarks by thanking you for acknowledging me. Of course, my remarks are always through the Chair. Maybe they should make their interruptions through the Chair; then 1 would not get in a straight line as the crow flies in responding to them.
The Hon. Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) pointed out how complex was this Bill and the oppressive atmosphere and environment it provided to the job-creating sector of Canada. Also we heard from the Hon. Member for Dart-mouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) about the confusion in the marine sector which these amendments and the tax legislation delivered. Complexity is there in spades.
1 was in the House through the budget of a former Minister of Finance, Mr. Turner. I was in the House and could not believe my ears when that man was asked what it was of which he was most proud in his capacity as Minister of Finance. He said: "I guess I am most proud of the one million jobs 1 have created". The people of Canada are paying the price for the creation of those types of jobs. In 1972, when they changed a basically simple tax Act to a complicated monster of paper, intrigue and purest academic thinking, they destroyed the decision-making base of people conducting widely diverse activities across Canada.
It is no longer possible to make a decision, even when one has lawyers and chartered accountants serving one's private sector entity in the boardroom. The amount of energy which is delivered to tax planning and tax management instead of to the essential productivity need of the nation is just a national disaster. It has delivered us the 1.5 million unemployed people we have today.
Our priorities are so screwed up, it does not seem that the Government has any way out. As I said last Friday, it is the result of a deliberate plan to move the state in and over all aspects of our lives and to remove the freedom of choice from the marketplace. If we want to see what they have done to the fundamental, natural law of supply and demand, all we have to do is look at the results delivered on the nation by their great academic, elitist, national energy policy. These elitists, these academics who have had no experience at all in the world of work, think they can plan everything from the centre and project their strategies over our future. They cannot even see three years ahead, so why do they keep hanging on to this mania that they have to allow academics, economists, engineers, socialist planners and national industrial strategists to plan our lives for the future?
The national energy policy just had the dot put on it in the last year and already it is obsolete. It has cost us jobs all across the country. The Government does not build infrastructures which will help create industries that will create jobs and allow us to participate in the marketplace. This Liberal Government keeps trying to interfere with the basic, natural law of supply and demand. Every time this Government does so, up goes the unemployment index in Canada. If you want to get back to a basic, fundamental truce, you have to get back to the basic, fundamental law of supply and demand. Had we stayed with the principle of supply and demand, we would have an energy policy in this country today that would be creating jobs, delivering the results of exploration efficiently and we would
Income Tax
be a landmark of success in comparison to the overview of the world economic down cycle.
Just like Reaganomics.

The Liberals have spent everything we collected in taxes. It was done all through the good times. This Government spends, spends and spends. It does not matter how the money is spent; this Government just likes to spend. It goes for borrowing Bills of $19 billion, $22 billion, $14 billion and $5 billion. Its policy is to spend and create debt. But all the Liberals are doing is lining their own pockets today at the expense of those who follow tomorrow.
Hear, hear!

The Government that has to take over this mess has a decade of the hardest work you can imagine, Mr. Speaker. That Government will have to do the most responsible type of work imaginable to pull this country back into some kind of a condition of sanity. The Liberal Party of Canada has a chain and an anchor around its neck for what it has done to this country and for the condition we are now in.
Let me review some of the budgets we have had. We had the Chretien budget. It took us all through our nine months to bring the Chretien budget elements into law because the ways and means were in place. We had a series of national disasters, the three MacEachen budgets. Now we have a very able-I have to say very able-Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) who has had to fix up the total chaos which the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) delivered on the people of this country. In fixing up this total chaos, do you have any idea of the absolute confusion that exists across this land, Mr. Speaker? Not even the lawyers or the chartered accountants can assist the wealth producers of this nation.
The Government delivers a budget and employs a tax collection system that is totally illegal. It has become a practice to do things without having a law in place. What we have done in this House is to let this Government collect taxes illegally. I have been told that the 1982 tax form has changed unilaterally, without authority from this Parliament, the dividend factor from 25 per cent to 22.66 per cent. I have been told that not only is that formula printed in the new forms, but the computer has been reprogrammed to accept a 22.66 per cent factor. But not a word about this was put out across the nation. Now the chartered accountants are struggling and wondering why their calculations do not work out. They find this subtle, dirty technique of silent change, without the authority of this House, has delivered us into this type of hidden taxation.
The Government moves in with a dividend tax on the small business community. What the Government has done has created absolute chaos. The money being spent across this land to move out of holding companies, which the Chretien budget created, is unbelievable.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Quit while you are ahead, Ron.

I see you are indicating that my time is coming to an end, Mr. Speaker, but let me state that confusion, crisis, chaos, disaster and subtlety is what we have. Nobody can trust this Government. We have taxation on taxation without law.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) certainly made some very worth-while points that we should be pursuing as a Government and as a Parliament. I hope Hon. Members who sit on the Government benches will take heed of what he has said.
It seems to me, as the Hon. Member who preceded me said so eloquently, that this Government is leaving the country in a mess. There is no question that this Government will be leaving office after the next election. 1 am sure if Hon. Members opposite want to be honest with themselves there is no question in their minds either that they will be leaving the Government benches, but 1 hope that between now and election time they will behave as responsibly as they can.
It seems to me there is an attitude prevalent on the Government benches which is getting worse each day. It seems the Government does not care what it does now because the mess it will leave will have to be cleaned up by somebody else. If that is the attitude and it continues like that, Liberal Members will be seen to be totally irresponsible.
Let me talk a little bit about the taxation system. First, a taxation system, if it is going to work at all, has to be fair. It has to be applied equally to everyone who pays tax. Our system is based on voluntary compliance.
Right on.

Everyone who speaks on this Bill says that Bill C-139 consists of 300 pages. But it is substantially larger than that because there are many pages in it numbered, "a". For instance, we have pages 118 and 118a. The Bill is probably closer to having 500 pages than 300 pages. Something like this, so large and so complex, is very difficult for people to understand and to comply with. Their reasons for wanting to comply with it become less and less. If we ever get into a situation in this country when people do not want to comply voluntarily with the Income Tax Act, we will have utter chaos. The more complicated a tax measure becomes, the more discriminatory it becomes. People who can afford to hire the best tax lawyers and accountants will be the ones who will be the best treated under the Act.
The Hon. Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) pointed out that in Canada we have more lawyers and accountants than we have research scientists. This just shows what this Government has done. It has not put emphasis on production, which should be the basis for a taxation system. We should have a system that is an incentive to produce rather than a disincentive.
Let me talk about a couple of principles and then 1 will refer specifically to two items in the Bill that I find most disheartening and discouraging. First, and this has been mentioned many times before, is the basic problem in the process we use to pass tax measures. Much uncertainty is created in how one calculates his or her tax. I have been in this House almost four years and there have been several changes within those four years, but none of them has been finalized, as I understand it, and put into law. This is what we will be doing when we finally pass Bill C-139, if in fact that happens. Unless you have some certainty with a tax measure, it is very difficult for people to comply with. That is the basic problem.
As I said, most Canadians voluntarily comply with the Income Tax Act. I think most Canadians feel they have an obligation to their country and an obligation to pay for the services the Government renders to them. But a tax system has to be fair. There has to be some kind of a belief that the redistribution of money which takes place after taxation is done fairly. People do not perceive that to be the case if tax Bills are so complicated and are being changed all the time. This leaves uncertainty and confusion in people's lives. They do not understand.
I have Bill C-143 before me. This is basically a tax Act. It is a method of spending. In it the Government is asking for authority to borrow money. It contains just two pages but it is asking for $19 billion. What you have is a two-page document to borrow $19 billion, and a document in excess of 300 pages to collect money which to me is unfair to the Canadian taxpayer. We have to understand a 300-page, complicated document to collect taxes while the Government produces a two-page document to borrow $19 billion. I question that. The Government has two pages to request authority to borrow and spend $19 billion but a document of more than 300 pages to collect money.
Let me use Section 12.2 as an example which was pointed out to me by the Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), who is very well acquainted with the Income Tax Act. Section 12.2(1) states:
In computing the income for a taxation year of a corporation, partnership, unit trust or any trust of which a corporation or partnership is a beneficiary that holds-
It goes on to mention those things that a corporation or partnership may hold:
-there shall be included the amount by which the accumulating fund at the end of the calendar year ending in the taxation year, as determined in prescribed manner, in respect of the interest exceeds the adjusted cost basis of the interest to the corporation, partnership, unit trust or trust at the end of that calendar year.
What that essentially means is that we will be taxed on accumulated or accrued income that we do not actually have in our hands. I believe that once the Government implements a measure such as that, it attacks the concept of private ownership in this country. The Government is saying through this Section that it owns everything and therefore has the authority to take money from the taxpayers that they have not even seen.
March 1, 1983

For example, if an individual takes out a life insurance policy that accrues in value over a period of time, that individual will have to pay a tax on that accrued income to the Government even though he has not seen the money. Once a tax like that is implemented-which the Government is attempting to do through this Section of the Bill-it means that the Government is attacking the very principle of private ownership. This Section will require an individual to find the money to pay a tax on the increased value of an instrument such as a life insurance policy. I suggest that a measure such as this has very serious implications for the direction in which this country is headed.
Another concern that I have with regard to the basic principle of income tax is that as the taxation system becomes more complex, the average taxpayer will have to spend more money to hire accountants and tax lawyers instead of concentrating on productively contributing to the country. Let me quote from Section 109 which implements paragraph 151 of the income tax motion. It states:
That a corporation be required to pay a special tax of 12.5 per cent on distributions made by it out of earnings in taxation years commencing after 1982 that were subject to the small business deduction under Subsection 125(1) of the Act and that rules be introduced to counter the avoidance of the tax.
That paragraph is very complicated. I defy any Member in the House to explain what I just read. I am told that it essentially means that the system by which the distribution of dividends will be made will be changed. This is a change from the Department of Revenue's previous proposal of going to an integrated system of tax in which the corporate rate of tax is adjusted to the individual rate of tax so that there can be no double taxation. It is now being changed in midstream with the result that it will be very difficult for people to understand what kind of tax they should pay.
The entire process by which this Bill has been introduced is backwards. As Members of Parliament, we should be using the committee system that is in place to draft these Bills so that they make common sense and can be understood. This procedure should be followed instead of giving the bureaucracy the powers that the House should have in terms of drafting legislation. Once legislation has been drafted by the bureaucrats and has been introduced and supported by the Government, it becomes very difficult to change a Bill. That procedure is exactly opposite to what I and most Canadians envisage as Parliament's function. We should not be reacting to what the civil servants have given us, which is the situation with this Bill. I do not believe the Minister alone is responsible for drafting this Bill; I submit that we are reacting to legislation that was drafted by bureaucrats.
I believe we should make proper use of the committee system. In this case, the Finance Committee should be the body that would review the tax policies in Canada and decide how they should be changed. Through that process, the legislation drafted by the committee can be brought to the House for debate and final approval.
The fact that the taxation system has become a disincentive to production represents another backward step. The taxation
Income Tax
system, rather, should create wealth and generate incentives. At that point the Government can concern itself with how taxes are distributed. Presently, this Government has bankrupt policies that spend us into oblivion. It then tries to determine how much money it can confiscate from Canadians for it to run some of its foolish and nonsensical schemes.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The Hon. Member for Oxford.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
Tory No. 66.

As shown by the Hon. Member opposite, it is clear how concerned Members opposite are about our tax system. We seem to hear very little from them about this entire issue. One must conclude that they agree with this complicated 295-page Bill C-139 which is before us today. Apparently they do not believe they have any responsibility as Government Members to intervene in this debate on behalf of their constituents and all Canadians in an attempt to point out the inadequacies and incomprehensibility of this Bill to the Government. Nor do they seem concerned about the total tax system.
I am disappointed to see that there are that many Members who feel that this Bill is not sufficiently important for them to speak. I am rather proud that there are 66 Members on this side who are concerned about this Bill and are prepared to speak about it in the House. I would venture to say that one of the advantages of parliamentary reform is that there is more opportunity and more responsibility for all of us to speak.
I have not been one to speak frequently in the House in the past because I do not think it is important to repeat what somebody else has said. However, I think it is incumbent upon all of us who represent our respective constituencies to get up and comment when we are faced with a tax Bill that is as inequitable as this one. More Members now have the opportunity to speak about Bills such as this before the Government has a chance to bring in some form of closure.
In the course of the last several months I have had well over 100 letters sent to me complaining about various parts of the three different budgets which have been brought down since the fall of 1981. The majority of complaints were from those who were upset about the provisions regarding the taxation of premiums paid on health and dental plans. Fortunately, because of the reaction from the public the Government has backed down from that provision. The Government should back down from much of what it has proposed in Bill C-139.
I believe there is a fundamental flaw in this Bill which should be addressed. My colleagues, the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) and the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), referred to it this morning. It refers to the fact that this Bill is totally incomprehensible. This fact was brought to our attention most effectively in a paper which was sent to us. It was a speech that was given by Mr. Lyman Maclnnis of the Touche, Ross Company. I dare say

March 1, 1983
Income Tax
that Members opposite have received the same document. The speech has been quoted previously in the House but I think it is important that Government Members be reminded of it so that they know what Mr. Maclnnis has said about our present tax system.
It appears that the present Government is not interested in trying to alleviate the difficulties that Mr. Maclnnis has illustrated in his paper about the tax system. He outlined three interesting problems in our tax system as he saw them. One problem related to the fact that, by the very nature of our present income tax system, the onus is upon the taxpayer to assess what tax he must pay. That method is different from most other taxes that we are forced to pay in this society. We have agreed to pay other taxes. For example, we pay sales tax, which is a predetermined amount that is paid with each purchase. We know what the tax is.
The other basic principle that we must acknowledge is that in order to be able to assess tax on our own, since we are not professionals in this area, the tax system must be clear and the language must be unmistakable. It must be possible for the average person to understand it.
Thirdly, now that our tax system is so complicated, many taxpayers must hire professionals to help them with their tax returns. The problem is that the very people who are least able to understand the complicated wording of the tax system are the very ones who need help the most and can least afford to pay for that help.
I think I can afford to devote a couple of minutes to reading what Mr. Maclnnis wrote in his paper with regard to the complexity of the wording in the present Act. Mr. Maclnnis quoted Section 56(1 )(s) as follows:
"Without restricting the generality of Section 3, there shall be included in computing the income of a taxpayer for a taxation year, the amount of any grant received in the year under a prescribed program of the Government of Canada relating to home insulation or energy conversion by the taxpayer, other than a married taxpayer who resided with his spouse at the time the grant was received and whose income for the year is less than his spouse's income for the year, or the spouse of the taxpayer with whom he resided at the time the grant was received, if the spouse's income for the year is less than the taxpayer's income for the year to the extent that the amount is not required by paragraph I2(l)(u) to be included in computing his or his spouse's income for the year or a subsequent year''.
That is but one paragraph, one little part of the Act, and it is completely incomprehensible.
If we look back in history a little to 1962, we find that it was acknowledged then that our tax system was very complicated and some changes were necessary. A Royal Commission was set up, and about ten years later the observations and recommendations with regard to the system translated into changes in the Income Tax which were supposedly to simplify and improve the ability of Canadian taxpayers to understand the Act. What we have before us today is the result of the work of the Royal Commission from 1962 onwards, culminating in the changes the Government introduced in 1971.
The Government has moved to complicate the Act even more and has not fulfilled the role which the Carter Commission was to have fulfilled. We were to have been given something which was more simple. However, this was based entirely on certain concepts and the Government jumped to a certain conclusion, namely, that "ability to pay" was a sound taxation principle. It seems to have entirely forgotten the concept that to be fair, the fact must also be taken into consideration that people are provided certain services under the umbrella of the state. There should therefore be a tax system which takes into account those two principles, the principle involving ability to pay as well as the principle that people should be required to pay something based on the kind of services received under the umbrella of the Government at the time. Of course, one can apply that to the three basic types of taxes: personal tax, business tax and property tax.
I see Your Honour is signalling that my allotted time has just about expired. I will conclude by saying that at a future date it would be well if we addressed the issues involving those three components of our tax system in relation to the concept of ability to pay, which is recognized now, as well as the concept of paying tax based on services received.

Mr. Speaker, if ever a nation needed a new tax Act and a new Government to administer it, it is this nation, now.
Some Eton. Members: Hear, hear!

We have seen our country abused by the tax system to the point at which the system could not be described in anything but obscene language, to which you, Mr. Speaker, would properly raise objection in the House. Therefore, I will not use the obscene language which is really necessary to describe our tax system. I will just imply that that is what is required.
We see a nation in economic difficulty, faced with an unemployment problem, and a Government which does not understand the difference between its own cash flow and so-called tax expenditures when extending a little privilege to a company. The difference the Government has never been able to understand concerning revenue expenditure versus its net income is that when incentive is not provided, unemployment is created.
That is precisely what the Government has done, budget after budget, with Turner being the apostle of deficit financing, excessive taxation and over-expenditure of public revenue. He started it, and he certainly converted the apostles who followed in the field of Government finance.
We need a new Income Tax Act and we need a new Government that understands where revenue comes from, that understands it comes from profitable companies, from a productively employed work force, from a striving, thriving economy, not one which is choked to death by one taxation structure after another as in this country.

Absolutely right.
March 1, 1983
And you sit there and grin, my friends?
Fleming.

Mr. Speaker, do not get worried; I would not waste my breath on him.
I received a call from a gentleman who is involved in the tax structure since he happens to be a chartered accountant. He said: "In my career as an accountant I have never seen people being stripped of their working capital as the Government is presently robbing them, directly and indirectly, of the working capital which is so badly needed".
Illegal, too.	'

He said: "I have never seen incentive being stripped along with the working capital as it is being stripped from the private sector in this day's society by the Government, with its successive budgets. I have never seen so many of my clients determined that they shall take whatever tax advantage they can, then take their money and retire very prematurely." He also said: "In my community, unemployment is increasing because people are taking their marbles, quitting the game and going home because of the disincentives resulting from what is happening here".
Concerning cash flow, the Government is prepared to assist Massey-Ferguson financially, but is not prepared to allow farmers to have the capital cost allowance to which they have been accustomed and which enabled them to buy farm equipment. The Government is prepared to back the Chrysler Corporation and the auto industry in general with hundreds of millions of dollars, but does everything possible to constrict the purchase of automobiles by removal of the capital cost allowance, by the change to the expense deductions of travellers, by the change in the opportunity to purchase executive cars. If there was ever an example of someone really trying to take advantage of it, it is myself. In my business and political career, I traded cars not less than every two years. My wife now has the use of one automobile which is five years old, and the one which I prefer to drive is four years old.
You are lucky, you have two cars.

There are at least six automobiles which I have not purchased on the consumer market because of the tax structure which has been imposed on the nation. The idiots can sit and laugh at the economic realities, but it was better for me to take 20 per cent interest on the trading money and keep the old car than it was to trade and have that money tied up in an automobile.
Hear, hear!

They laugh while the unemployed autoworkers starve. That may be funny, but they should ask the gentleman from Oshawa what he thinks about that kind of idiocy.
I abhor the idea that we have goons in the National Revenue Department going through files as far back as five, six, eight and ten years to see what a fisherman's income was and
Income Tax
whether he paid his taxes. What did the fisherman use for bait in his lobster traps and what was his expense? These goons go back four years and say to a fisherman that his expenses for lobster bait were excessive, and he cannot satisfactorily substantiate them. Fishermen had 300 lobsters in the water and are allowed depreciation on those traps, but are not allowed anything for the expense of baiting them. The Department of Fisheries established a figure in a particular year. I asked the then Minister what it cost to bait a lobster trap and was told that the cost was estimated at $15 per trap. The fisherman was allowed no cost for baiting his lobster traps on his return so there is $4,500 at an absolute minimum on which he is now being asked to pay back taxes. That is a goon type of collection system.
What is the situation with the farmer or the fellow who is trying to become a farmer in Prince Edward Island or New Brunswick, working at a job while trying to establish himself on a farm? He is considered as a hobby farmer. The Revenue officials go back four, five, six and eight years and say that this individual never made any money while trying to get into the farming business, so it is a hobby farm and he cannot be allowed any expenses in that regard. This individual is then told he owes taxes for that four, five, six or eight years. This policy is sucking the incentive out of the guy who wants to be a farmer, and there are many in P.E.I. and New Brunswick who do want to be farmers and are working day and night to get there. Yet these goons from the tax Department reassess them and take the incentive from these guys who have saved for years.
Let us suppose one of these individuals wants to appeal. He does not like what has been done. Such an individual in New Brunswick finds that he has been assessed in St. John's, Newfoundland. That is where the assessment or the revision of the tax requirement has been made. The individual appeals and all at once finds that he is addressing his appeal to no one else but the guy who did the reassessment. How is he going to win? He has no reasonable access to the courts and is merely appealing the assessment of one civil servant to another, and they all seem to be covering up their tails very nicely. In this way one will not appear to be making a mistake that can be overruled by another. The success rate of appeals from these reassessments is idiotically lacking. These people are being punished by a greedy Government with this group of people in place. For God's sake, I wonder if they are working on commission. They are certainly working without mercy as they assess or reassess fishermen, farmers and foresters.
We need a new tax Act and all the patches the Government can put on the present Act will never correct the inequities that have been brought about by irresponsible individuals who are described by the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) as people who perhaps have never had to work in the open marketplace and seem to be pretty determined that no one else shall thrive in that area.

March I, 1983
Income Tax
A chartered accountant said that we ought to give this Bill the attention it deserves. He said the place for it is the garbage can, and that is the attention it deserves. The Government should be asked to start over and bring in something that is definitive and understandable. This chartered accountant deplores the idea that people should be targeted as groups and that goon squads should go out to investigate the good work people have done. He deplores the fact that it is no longer the concept of the Canadian Government that one should be able to make out his own income tax return.
The initial concept of income tax was that it should be simple, there should be rates and certain deductions spelled out. There should be a single sheet income tax return so that any high school graduate would be competent to assess his own tax liability. In the early days there were very few reassessments.
We now have something which makes it impossible for the individual to file honestly. If he tries to file his return himself he is penalized and eventually has to go to an expert chartered accountant, or some other member of the accounting group, to bail him out of the interpretation that is placed on his return. The individual files the return honestly, but often the return is not acceptable to those who re-inspect, re-evaluate and reassess, and then stand firm on that reassessment without appeal. These people do not understand how to use the courts properly and are victimized in this situation. We need a new Act.

Mr. Speaker, 1 think this may be the first opportunity I have had to congratulate you on the appointment to the position you now hold. As a New Brunswicker I take great pride in having the opportunity to do that.
When asked to provide a list of the changes that had been made to budgetary measures since November of 1981, the Department of Finance simply stated it had no such list. No wonder; there have been 47 changes to the November, 1981 budget.
One welcome change is that the Government will not tax employee health and dental benefits as originally planned. Another is that the implementation of the shift in the manufacturers' sales tax to the wholesale level is to be delayed until mid-1984. In the interim, the Government has indicated that it will work with industry to explore ways of modifying the proposals.
Bill C-139 now before us seeks to implement many of the hodge-podge of Government measures, and it is one of the most complex tax Bills since the introduction of the 1971 reforms. The hardest hit by this Bill will be low and middle-income Canadians who will gain little or nothing from the lowering of marginal tax breaks, and who will lose proportionately more from partial deindexation.
The taxation of housing loans will make it hard to recruit employees who must relocate. For those who already have loans, a taxation of this benefit may represent a rude shock that was not anticipated when the employee accepted a housing loan as part of a relocation package.
The restrictions of owner participation in deferred profitsharing plans will discourage the owners of small firms from offering to their employees a plan for which they themselves are not eligible.
In its analysis, issued November 13, 1981, the accounting firm of Coopers & Lybrand suggested that the most disturbing thing about the November budget was its anti-business bias and its doctrinaire opposition to any form of tax relief and deferral.
The November budget attacked business as if it were a dreaded disease instead of being the principal force for economic growth and job creation. That budget eliminated many incentives for investment. Each of these incentives was originally placed in the Income Tax Act to encourage entrepreneurial activity and investment.
For example, the half-year convention will limit the capital cost allowance depreciation to half the normal rate in the year that an asset is purchased. This will significantly reduce the cash flow of a firm in the year that an asset is purchased. It will discourage capital investment at a time when the economy is in dire need of stimulus. It will hinder the retooling of Canadian manufacturers as they face the challenge of the 1980s.
Until the November budget, companies could make interest-free loans to employees to enable them to purchase shares in the companies for which they work. The taxation of benefits resulting from share purchase loans will reduce the healthy trend toward employee share ownership.
In November, 1981 the budget transformed the Small Business Development Bond from a development vehicle to a bail-out vehicle. Firms seeking financing from the Small Business Bonds are often faced with an interesting catch-22 situation. Financing is only available to firms in financial difficulty, but, as the bonds are not Government-guaranteed, the banks may not lend money to such businesses.
The November, 1981 budget proposed to end the immediate write-off, in full, of soft costs incurred prior to completion of construction. These include such expenses as promotion, legai and accounting fees, mortgage fees and interim interest expenses. These costs must now be capitalized and written off at the same rate as a building. Soft costs such as these are incurred in the construction of new factories, new wings for motels and new warehouses and, as in the case of a multiple unit residential building, they must now be capitalized.
Every time a new job is created, a new taxpayer is also created. If the 1.5 million Canadians who are now unemployed were put to work and over a period of years they paid $10,000 each in income tax, our revenues would swell by $15 billion. Our Unemployment Insurance and social justice payments would diminish radically so that those moneys too could be used for the betterment of all Canadians.
As I come to the conclusion of my short remarks, I would like to leave with the House for consideration two thoughts. At
March 1. 1983

the corporate level, what if small businesses starting up in areas suffering from regional disparities were provided a 150 per cent tax credit to cover capital costs and labour costs for the first three years of operation? I am not talking here about an outright grant. I am speaking rather of allowing a newly-established or expanded firm to apply these expenses against future income tax payable, thus providing the investor with an opportunity to recover his investment plus 50 per cent, and his labour cost for the first three years plus 50 per cent. We would in this way create a new corporate taxpayer and ensure the creation of badly needed jobs, all without taking a cent from the federal Treasury, simply delaying the payment of taxes.
What if the capital gains tax were abolished? The enormous administrative costs which presently attach to the collection of these revenue already considerably offset any perceived fiscal advantage. Even if we accepted at face value the $400 million which the Government presently collects in capital gains tax, I would argue that the advantages of eliminating this tax in terms of potential domestic and foreign investment and the consequent creation both of jobs and of new individual and corporate taxpayers would be overwhelming.
I would urge the Government to study these two proposals and ascertain whether it feels, as 1 do, that they are worth looking at and could be feasible ways of bringing in new taxpayers and increasing our revenues with resultant benefits to all Canadians. This Bill in its present form reminds me of a nest of mosquitoes with a number of annoying bites. It should instead have been used to create a climate attractive to industrial development.

Mr. Speaker, one thing I can say about Government Members not participating in the debate is that it certainly raises the quality of debate in the House of Commons. Quality of debate is a concern of people in my area. Bill C-139 is also a concern to people in Peace River country because it affects them so dramatically.
Yesterday in the House we spent some time debating the largest borrowing Bill in Canadian history. Today we are speaking about one of the largest economic Bills to come before us, 290 pages long. It makes a person wonder why the Government does not concentrate a little more on quality and less on quantity. This is especially true when one remembers that all 290 pages of this Bill are simply amendments to the tax Act. It is not a new Act, not a better one, but a confusing collection of amendments that I hesitate to call fine tuning.
This is especially true when one remembers that budgets are so crucial to the investment in, and well-being of, Canada. We can see that this Government does not intend to improve the investment climate or allow Canadians to plan for their future. This Government has made little attempt to make the tax Act rational. It has in fact made it harsher. It has adopted forward averaging and now you have to guess where you will be. It is reducing the capital cost allowance and plugging the loopholes. In many cases the Government is in fact creating taxes where there were no previous taxes. For example, if you have a company car, a company loan or a life insurance policy, you
Income Tax
are going to be looking at some taxes. You will in fact pay more tax and pay it more often.
The question that remains is whether the Government is in fact changing its mind about what Canadians should be encouraged to do. In the past, interest on loans to purchase RRSPs was deductible. That is no longer the case. This Bill reduces the dividend tax credit and restricts deductions for tuition fees. What we are finding is that these activities, where promoted in the past, are now not being promoted. We reduced the tax that you would have paid had you participated in the programs previously.
The Bill has made a complicated situation worse. Several of my colleagues have mentioned that fact. Many Canadians will need a good deal of help to do the Government's paper work, to do their own taxes. Payment for this help is not tax deductible for the majority of the Canadian people.
This Government will still insist that it be paid. Bill C-139 provides that the Government may garnishee money owed the taxpayer 90 days in advance of the funds becoming due to the taxpayer; in other words, an advance garnishee. We also find that if taxes are in arrears, Revenue Canada can seize the business and run it for the benefit of the taxes. Revenue Canada will become the bankruptcy initiator of Canada. It makes me shudder to think of Revenue Canada grabbing companies across Canada. Who will do business with these seized companies? How well will the bureaucrats run them? Who will decide when they can be grabbed? That is probably the most fundamental question to be faced. What do we think this will mean in terms of this new power when Canadians are already disenchanted with federal policies and the authoritarian actions of this Government?
This Bill gives with one hand and takes with the other. For example, we have the lower marginal tax rates, but on the other hand we have deindexing for inflation. The next budget will probably end the giving but do nothing about the taking. It is a vicious circle. Maybe they will take a different tack altogether and make it a highly political budget. That will give the Government a chance to play hero by reducing the marginal tax rate every year, something which the inflation index in the tax Act did automatically.
I have to say that this Bill will do some good. First, RRSPs can be divided on marriage breakdown. Second, and this is fairly significant in my area, travelling expenses for medical reasons are given a more reasonable tax deduction. Many people in my area live 300 miles from medical specialists and must incur once or twice a month heavy and dramatic medical travel costs. A man in my riding now cannot write off such medical expenses. Perhaps with this legislation he will. That is an important measure in the Bill.
Why stop there? Why not go the extra step to meet the basic needs of Canadians? The prime reason for having a Government is to look after the Canadian people, not to put stumbling blocks in front of them, as is the case with so much of this Bill. Much more is needed to make the tax system a reasonable system for Canadians.
