I want to give another example. In my area many farmers now have to hold down two jobs. This is particularly true with new farmers. They want one job because they want to farm, but they need the other one to make ends meet, to allow them to farm. In many instances, the income from the second job goes directly into the farm. They are making an investment in machinery, an investment in land improvement, which is very important in order to bring new land onstream, and an investment in livestock, their future capital base. They are making personal sacrifices to make their farms and their country a better place, yet the Income Tax Act actually penalizes them for their sacrifices.
If their income from the "other" job is greater than 50 per cent of the farm's income, they can only use something which has been called a "restricted farm loss". In fact, they are limited to a maximum deduction of $5,000. We all know that in today's farming business, particularly when you are trying to establish a new farm, $5,000 is peanuts. If the restricted farm loss had been tied to inflation, the figure would be significantly more equitable. In fact, it would be somewhere in the area of $20,000, not the insignificant $5,000 which farmers are given at the moment. Farm costs have risen so dramatically over the last five years that something must be done to encourage both new farmers and established farmers who are forced to seek income from other employment in order to maintain their farm as a viable operation.
Bill C-139 could recognize the inequities of the old Act. The Government could bring this restricted farm loss up to a viable level, it could index it to inflation, or it could even raise the ceiling for income from other sources. If nothing is done this investment in a very important sector of the economy-and it is certainly important in terms of the young farmers of the country-is going to grind to a halt. If we look at the average age of our farmers in Canada today, we find it is very high, around the age of 50. We must start bringing in new young farmers and the only way we are going to accomplish that is by making farming attractive and by encouraging them, rather than coming out with legislation that stifles their incentive and forces them to change their dreams and move from the country into the city.
I would like to remind the Government of three essential matters which fall under its responsibility towards Canadians. First, Canadians should be able to understand the laws which govern them. That is a very simple and basic right which Canadians should be able to expect. Second, Canadians should be encouraged to do the things which would improve their lot, and which in turn would improve the lot of this country. Third, the Government must, in terms of its responsibility towards the citizens of Canada, ensure that it is not too difficult for them to do those things which seem correct, and a simple example of that is my illustration of the farms in my own area.
Bill C-139 does not do any of these things, neither does it improve the present Act. This Government should be a good
Government and not one that reduces Canadians to dependence on their Government.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on the second reading of Bill C-139, an Act to amend the Income Tax Act. Last December 7, this Government finally introduced the income tax legislation necessary to implement the November, 1981 budget. It took 389 days to introduce this Bill, a mammoth 600-page document. It has been said, Mr. Speaker, that if you give enough typewriters to enough monkeys, in time the law of averages will allow them to create a masterpiece. Certainly the Government has enough typewriters. We know they have enough monkeys. I believe they just ran out of time, sir.
At present there are four major revisions of the November, 1981 budget: the original budget itself; the budget as amended in December, 1981; the June, 1982 version; and the October 27, 1982 version. In addition, there have been minor announcements and clarifications on several occasions, such as the January, 1982 announcement of employee benefits. There have been extensive consultations outside this House as well as the debate within this Chamber on the provisions of the ill-conceived budget of November, 1981. On that point, I would like to give credit where credit is due and say I respect the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) for going across the country to find out what people really have to say. Only time will tell, Mr. Speaker, whether or not the Minister listened.
There are many defects in this budget. I hope the present Minister of Finance will hear what my colleagues have had to say and take corrective measures before the Bill goes to committee. The Government seems to be listening and consulting, but despite the fact that there have been changes, the Government has not yet responded fully. Quite frankly, in reflecting upon all the wasted time and trouble which resulted from the original budget, the former Minister of Finance should have simply recognized the folly of his own budget, scrapped it and started over again from scratch. Neither he nor the present Minister of Finance has chosen to do this, which is precisely why we find ourselves in our present economic mess.
Bill C-139 is one of the most complex tax Bills since the introduction of the 1971 tax reforms. I have had an opportunity to wade through it, Mr. Speaker, and I would like to take this opportunity to address my remarks to specific examples showing which Canadians will be affected. The hardest hit will be low and middle-income Canadians. These are the Canadians who have been hit during the last 15 years of Liberal administration. They will gain little or nothing from the lowering of marginal tax rates and will lose proportionately more from partial deindexation.
The increased taxation of employee benefits will hit hardest those in the lower and middle income brackets. It will encourage employees to seek higher wage settlements at a time when moderation is indeed required. There are many examples in which employees have been receiving wage settlements in

excess of the Government's own six and five restraint program. The taxation of housing loans will make it harder to recruit employees who must relocate in order to retain their jobs. For those who already have loans, the taxation of this benefit will represent a rude shock which was not anticipated when the employee accepted a housing loan as part of his relocation offer.
Limitations on retiring allowances, termination benefits, and the $1,000 pension income deduction will make it harder for many Canadians to prepare for their retirement years. The restrictions on owner participation in deferred profit-sharing plans will discourage owners from offering a plan to their employees for which they themselves are not eligible.
The proposed taxation of the work-in-progress of professionals has been withdrawn, as outlined under Section 125 of the Income Tax Act. This will affect doctors, lawyers, accountants, dentists, veterinarians and chiropractors. This measure, however, remains in effect for engineers, architects and management consultants. That indeed, sir, is a discriminatory measure. It will create an administrative and tax burden on those professionals who must not only estimate the value of their work in progress, but pay tax on work which has yet to be billed.
A provision of this Bill which I find particularly disturbing is the removal of some of the secrecy provisions of the Income Tax Act. Revenue Canada will now be able to share tax information with other federal and provincial officials for the enforcement of exploration programs, for compiling statistical information, and for enforcing the Unemployment Insurance Act or other prescribed employment programs. These are only a few of the many changes to the Act which will affect countless Canadians from coast to coast.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canadians were shocked and somewhat angered by the recent United States Government decision to label as "political propaganda" three National Film Board films, two on the subject of acid rain and one on the subject of nuclear arms. This silly and ill-thought-out decision taken by our American friends represents poor judgment on the part of the United States administration, and can serve no useful purpose.
If our two countries have problems, and they do, then surely the way to deal with these problems is by open and direct dialogue. Moves such as labelling films produced by the National Film Board "political propaganda" serve only to dismay those of us who support open and free Government, and invite greater criticism from America's opponents.
The Canadian Government must register its concern with Washington and urge that greater caution and sensitivity be used in the future. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I bring to the attention of the House a recurring northern Ontario problem related to the operations of the CNR. The problem to which I refer is known as the Nakina run-through proposal.
Simply stated, railway companies have determined that frequent crew changes are no longer required as they were in the age of steam. While this may be true in general, there are some exceptions. Northern Ontario, with its more severe weather conditions, the monotony of running a train through a seemingly endless coniferous corridor, and the difficulties associated with track and roadbed maintenance, are all good reasons for the continuation of a crew change at Nakina.
During the early 1970s the CNR got one foot in the door by gaining agreement to run-through one freight train per day. Based on this experience it argues that its point has been proved. This is not so, say railroaders, because this one freight train is being given a priority by train masters.
In 1964 the Nakina run-through proposal led to a wildcat strike and an inquiry which gave us the Freedman Report. Unions are now obliged to negotiate with the company the terms of a run-through on behalf of members who are adversely affected, but the unions remain strongly opposed to the Nakina run-through.

SUGGESTED CHANGES TO STUDENT LOANS PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Canada Student Loans Program is supposed to give all Canadians a better chance to get a college education or to get the training necessary to find a job in our technologically advanced society. At the present time the Program is failing on both counts.
High interest rates and a 22 per cent youth unemployment rate are very real barriers to kids from working class families who want an education but worry about being saddled with a large debt and no way to pay it back after graduation.
Also, the exclusion of part-time students from eligibility under the plan makes it impossible for many unskilled workers and single parents to improve their training while taking care of their other responsibilities. I therefore call on the Government to take positive action on two counts to call a moratorium on student loan interest charges for recent graduates who are unable to find work, and to review the loans Program to allow part-time students to get federal assistance to attend school and upgrade their skills.

Alberta holds the view that the 75 per cent rule was meant to protect Canadian consumers against ever escalating prices of world energy, that they were not meant to protect the Canadian consumer against the hypothesis of falling energy prices.
It is an honest disagreement on the meaning of the agreement we have with Alberta. The Premier has expressed his views, and we have expressed ours.

Madam Speaker, I am not asking the Prime Minsiter for his interpretation of what the accord meant. I am asking him to give a commitment in terms of his Government's policy, not the policy of the Government of Alberta. Will he tell the House unequivocally that, if world prices continue to go down, the commitment made by
his then Minister of Energy, concurred in by the Minister of Energy from Alberta in the communique, on Canadian competitiveness in international markets, will be maintained so we will get badly needed jobs for Canadians who are out of work?
No vacillating.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I hear support for that point of view from the Tory benches. I can assure the House that we will need support from all sides of the House.
You need support from everyone.

Exactly; particularly from the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West, because I can recall when that Province was led by an NDP Premier, the NDP Members of this House were not as vocal as they are today in imposing unilaterally on the Province our interpretation of the agreement. I just say I can give that commitment in so far as our intentions are concerned and in so far as the policy as we see it. But the Hon. Member has to realize that there was an agreement between the Province of Alberta and the Government of Canada. I think the Leader of the New Democratic Party would be the first to blame me if I gave him the assurance that I will impose my view of that agreement without considerating the view of the Province of Alberta.
It was Alberta's view on September 18.

subtopic: APPEARANCE IN GALLERY OF ONTARIO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

subtopic: APPEARANCE IN GALLERY OF ONTARIO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I welcome Members of the Public Accounts Committee of the Province of Ontario, chaired by Mr. Patrick Reid, who are seated in our gallery.

subtopic: APPEARANCE IN GALLERY OF ONTARIO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. For some time now there has been a critical problem regarding approximately 1,000 Iranian students in Canada whose funding has been cancelled by the Iranian Government. They are unable to return to Iran for fear of repression. Could the Minister tell the House what steps he is now ready to take to assist in this serious problem and allow these Iranian students to stay in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF IRANIAN STUDENTS IN CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, since 1979 and the major
March 1, 1983

upheavals in Iran we have not taken any steps to deport or send people back to Iran. It looks quite clear that conditions will not change in the immediate future. We will apply the same special measures to the 2,000-odd Iranians in the country, including the 1,000 students whom the Hon. Member mentioned, as we have applied to the Salvadorans, Lebanese, and Polish groups. That means that if they have families in this country they can apply for landed status or, if they have been here for a 12-month period and can demonstrate some capacity to settle in the country, we will also provide for landing. I hope that this will be a proper response to the difficult situation faced by those groups, particularly the students, and that we will be able to protect their human rights in that circumstance.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. He indicated in his earlier answer to the Hon. Member for Etibocoke Centre that he is waiting for an economic recovery to bail us out of our economic crisis. At the same time, however, the fastest growing envelope for Government spending is not job creation measures or social safety nets; it is the public debt which has grown from 12.6 per cent to 20 per cent of total outlays in just four years. How does the Minister justify his bid to borrow another $19 billion when the Estimates show that no serious attempt has been made to constrain Government spending?

Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member, who has a background in economics, ought to know that a recession is not the right time to try and balance a budget or have a budget surplus. In a recession like the one we have just experienced, it is perfectly normal that the Canadian Government should have a substantial deficit. That deficit is due to well known cyclical factors, namely a very substantial increase in unemployment and lower government revenues as a result of a drop in the amount of taxes paid by corporations and individuals. So this is a generally known strategy that is supported by economists throughout the world as an anti-recession strategy, and I am surprised that my hon. colleague should be concerned about this.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is also directed to the Minister of Finance. I am glad that he admits that it was the Liberal Government's strategy to take a $10 billion deficit into this recession to start with.
Oral Questions
How does the Minister of Finance justify a 17 per cent increase in Government spending, as shown by his own figures in the Estimates, when the Government has imposed 6 per cent and 5 per cent restraints on old age pensioners, civil servants, and families receiving Family Allowances?

Madam Speaker, the figures in the Estimates that were tabled last week represent an increase of 9.6 per cent over expenditures for 1982-83. Now I would like to ask my hon. colleague the following question. Does she feel that the Government should stop paying interest on Canada Savings Bonds, which were purchased by Canadians. Should the Government refuse to pay its share of medical insurance, health insurance, unemployment insurance and welfare payments which are now helping millions of Canadians who are in need? If that is the position of the Progressive Conservative Party, I would understand, but I can assure the Hon. Member that it is not the position of this Government.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Revenue. Since Fort Erie is in my riding and is the largest single vehicular point of entry, when does the Minister plan to open one of these overland duty-free stores in the town of Fort Erie in my riding?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT DUTY-FREE STORE BE OPENED IN FORT ERIE, ONT.
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we, that is, my predecessor and myself, negotiated the establishment of duty-free shops as a pilot project. Most of the provinces negotiated with us in good faith, and we were able to agree on the sale of liquor in those shops. Unfortunately, we were unable to reach an agreement with the Government of Ontario. I suggest that the Hon. Member get in touch with the Government of the Province of Ontario and urge it to follow the example of other provinces and thus negotiate a satisfactory agreement with the Canadian Government with respect to the sale of alcohol in duty-free stores on the border between Ontario and the United States.

Madam Speaker, if the Minister receives a favourable response from the Province of Ontario, is

March 1, 1983
Oral Questions
he then committing himself to opening a store in the town of Fort Erie in my riding?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I understand the Hon. Member's concern for his own riding. I also imagine that there are many Members from Ontario who are equally interested in having a duty-free store in their ridings. I shall bear the Hon. Member's representation in mind, and I hope that he will manage to persuade the Government of Ontario to reach an agreement with us.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. Due to the importance of the issue I have given the Minister notice of the question. I would ask him to explain to the House why Air Canada promoted and sold discount seat sales before it had prior approval from the CAB and, in view of another deadline coming in this mess, what is the present status?

Madam Speaker, the system that exists now is fairly clear. Carriers can advertise and, when they do, they have to say "subject to the approval of the Government of Canada". They then have to file and then they can subsequently sell. That is the system. It is clear.
The justification for this system is simply the rules of competition, the requirements of marketing. If a company comes out with a sale such as the one Air Canada had, it wants to be first. The need to be first is part of the competition. The system is also predictable.
Are you making plans on a predictable basis?

Yes. It is a predictable system because in most instances, 90 per cent or more, these special discounts go through. In this particular instance, the one we are concerned with, it was approved by the CTC as my hon. friend knows. It was also approved in principle by CAB in the United States. If my hon. friend read the documents he will know that they approved it. What they did after was to tie their approval to a condition concerning another company. So, what was unpredictable was the behaviour of the Americans in this particular instance.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER TALK TO UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER TALK TO UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in order to bring some certainty and predictability to this very confused situation I wish to direct my supplementary question to the Prime Minister. Knowing full well that the Prime Minister and the President of the United States fly from
country to country without CAB or CTC approval, and since it is clearly not competition but the use of innocent Canadian travellers as pawns in a regulatory fight between Canada and the United States, would he pick up the phone, if he has not already done so, and talk to his counterpart in the United States, President Reagan, to see if the CAB prohibition could be eliminated, that Canadians can travel, and that the two countries can work out their differences without using innocent Canadians as pawns?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER TALK TO UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I can assure the Hon. Member that on this side of the House I have full confidence in the capabilities of my Ministers, and particularly in this case, of the Minister of Transport.

Madam Speaker, my question is also directed to the Prime Minister. As he knows, yesterday the Metis associations from western Canada walked out of the meeting of the Attorneys General on the Constitution. The position that has been taken by the Metis associations is that they are not represented by Metis at the First Ministers' Conference coming up on March 15 and 16. Will the Prime Minister act to guarantee that there will be seats for the Metis spokesmen at that Conference?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have not been briefed on all the details of what happened yesterday but I can assure the Hon. Member that, when I sent out invitations to that Conference, I sent them out to official groups representing the Inuit, Metis, and Indian population. Therefore, the three aboriginal groups were invited to the Conference.
I know that within the Metis themselves there was a jurisdictional quarrel which, I was informed, had been solved previous to yesterday's meeting. However, if there are further difficulties we will try to assist in solving them. I would point out to the Hon. Member that it is up to the Metis themselves to decide first and foremost who should speak for them. It would be quite paternalistic if the Government were to designate the spokesmen for the Metis people as though they could not make their own choice themselves.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Defence. I have received U.S. Army documents dealing with the technical
March 1, 1983

co-operation program between Canada, the United Kingdom, the U.S. and Australia. Under this program, chemical biological and radiation weapon systems were tested and developed in Alberta, Saskatchewan, Newfoundland, and elsewhere. The documents quite clearly show that they were offensive attack purposes and involved tests concerning the spread of yellow fever, botulism, tuberculosis, genetic engineering, anti-crop agents, et cetera. I have passed this information and copies of the documents over to the Minister.
Will the Minister confirm that Canada was involved in the testing of offensive biological, chemical, and radiation weapons of war, and is he prepared to clear the public record by tabling in the blouse or before a parliamentary inquiry all documentation, past and present, relating to Canada's work on these weapons, before we start testing the Cruise missile?
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member for Regina East is asking a question that deals somewhat with history. The policy of this Government as far as biological or chemical warfare is concerned is very clear. In 1925 we signed an international Convention prohibiting biological and chemical warfare. This policy formed part of the 1972 Geneva protocol. At the moment, in Geneva, we are pursuing the complete prohibition of stockpiling and production of any and all chemical weapons. This is still an issue before the disarmament committee in Geneva. It is true, however, that we as a country, including myself as Minister of National Defence, are burdened with the responsibility of protecting, by all possible means, our own soldiers and our own people against a possible attack of this nature by other peoples.
Chemical warfare?
When we test this weaponry or do in fact make some use of it, we do so strictly on a defensive or protective basis; that is, to protect our own soldiers, just in case something happens.

subsubtopic: WOMEN'S REPRESENTATION AT FORTHCOMING CONFERENCE-POSSIBILITY OF SUBSEQUENT MEETING ON ECONOMY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Right Hon. Prime Minister. speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: WOMEN'S REPRESENTATION AT FORTHCOMING CONFERENCE-POSSIBILITY OF SUBSEQUENT MEETING ON ECONOMY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in answer to the first part of the Hon. Member's question, my answer would be similar to the answer I gave with regard to the question of the Metis representation. However, I do not believe it is for the federal Government to designate the members of the delegations of the Provinces, of the Territories, or of the native people. We know that there will be women present on some of the delegations and, indeed, at the table in certain instances. Of course 1 cannot say, because I cannot dictate to the participants who their representatives should be, whether women will be on the delegations or not.
As to the second part of the Hon. Member's question, I did contact the Provinces to suggest that, since we were all in town for a constitutional conference, we should spend a few hours together discussing the economy. The Ministers of Finance of the Provinces and of the federal Government will be meeting next week. They may have some questions they want to refer to us, but they will certainly be considering short-term questions, because discussions will be in the context of the upcoming budgets of the Provinces and of the federal Government. I would hope that the provincial Premiers and myself would have some time to consider medium and longer term questions on the economy. 1 suggested an evening meeting, but 1 am open to counter suggestions by the Premiers with regard to the time.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. subsubtopic: ANNOUNCED CLOSURE OF CANADA PACKERS PLANT IN CHARLOTTETOWN, P.E.L
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister responsible for regional development. subsubtopic: ANNOUNCED CLOSURE OF CANADA PACKERS PLANT IN CHARLOTTETOWN, P.E.L

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT CANADIAN CONTENT LEGISLATION BE ENACTED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister responsible for international trade, and concerns jobs. About two weeks ago General Motors and Toyota signed an agreement to produce Japanese cars in California, providing about 12,000 jobs, directly or indirectly, to American citizens. In light of the fact that we are once again negotiating with respect to Japanese autos, and that past negotiations have failed in terms of Canadian content, I wonder whether the Minister would consider, in order to give himself some more bargaining power, introducing in this House, for first reading, a Canadian content Bill before negotiations continue on a very serious basis, so the Japanese
March 1, 1983

will see that we are serious about Canadian jobs here in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerald Regan (Minister of State (International Trade)):
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT CANADIAN CONTENT LEGISLATION BE ENACTED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am glad to know that the Hon. Member is thinking about jobs, because I believe all Canadians are particularly concerned about that. I want to say to him, through you, most seriously that my first responsibility as Minister of Trade is to create Canadian jobs by the export of Canadian goods.
During all our discussions about autos the Hon. Member should keep in mind that we are selling record levels of Canadian goods abroad today, and that Japan is an extremely important and large customer. Our trade with Japan is very much in our favour. Let us keep in mind, first of all, that our negotiations should be carried on in such a way as to protect the Canadian jobs that exist. Having said that, we will be going back to the table with Japan for the remaining portion of this year and for a further time period, in the near future. At that time we will be negotiating the allowed levels of imports. I may say to the Hon. Member that protectionism in respect of auto content or the content of any other product is not in the Canadian interest as a free trade exporting country.

Madam Speaker, the Minister talks about free trade. I wonder if he really knows what the Japanese are like as negotiators. Japan is a country that now has an unemployment rate of some 2.3 per cent. I want to ask the Minister specifically, if he is interested in creating jobs in this country, would he not consider introducing, for first reading at least, a Canadian content Bill. If he does not want to do that, will he tell us specifically what his goals are in negotiating with the Japanese? What is the bottom line? Is he going to make sure that there will be the development of Japanese cars in this country with at least 85 per cent Canadian content?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerald Regan (Minister of State (International Trade)):
speechtext:
First of all. Madam Speaker, I want to tell the Hon. Member that if we start legislating something like auto content or protective measures, then the other countries with which we trade will enact the same sort of legislation. Export markets are immensely important to Canada with our great resources, our products, and our small population. We, of all people, should not be putting up barriers of protectionism. When we are negotiating with the Japanese we will be negotiating on the basis of seeking their investment in this country, yes, but, above all, of determining the number of vehicles that will come in. I might point out to the Hon. Member that some of the area of responsibility with which he is concerned, which is investment in this country, falls within the area of responsibility of my colleague, the Minister of Industry. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we engage in this debate, as we do with so many things these days, with a sense of bitterness and frustration. Where did they go, those bright promises of 1980, those bright
promises of the years ahead? The bright hopes and undertakings with which this Government entered office have turned to broken dreams, scuppered promises, unfulfilled projects and benefits forgotten.
As we came into the House today, sir, we had the catastrophic news of a drop in the Gross National Product, the sum total of all the goods and services provided by Canadians. The drop is in the order of 5 per cent. That is the worst showing in domestic production since 1933. In that year, 1933, we were at the height of the Great Depression, with its soup kitchens, its bonus marchers, its farm foreclosures, its bank failures and its general despair. Instead of stimulating the economy, this Government has been hamstringing it. Instead of encouraging investment, this Government has closed the door to investment. Instead of allowing the private sector to do what it does best, which is provide jobs for Canadians, this Government has followed interventionist courses of curtailing, confining and milking the private sector of incentive and, of course, resources.
In the energy field alone this Government dropped 10,000 jobs by default when it fumbled Alsands, when it fumbled the Alaska Highway natural gas pipe line and other megaprojects that would have provided the lifeline that the economy so sorely needed. It dropped the megaprojects but went on with the Gillespie project which had the recommendation that none of the others had-it had that special urgency that comes when Liberals are dealing with Liberals. Day after day our Members have risen in this House to bring to the attention of the Government the attrition brought about in individual ridings by a collapsing economy.
In Ottawa this week, making the rounds of Ministers' offices, there has been a delegation of outstanding citizens from my riding of Yukon. They are seeking some slight sign of interest or initiative with regard to the reopening of the Cyprus-Anvil mine at Faro, a major employer in Yukon that contributes 40 per cent of the economy of that part of the country. The Japanese are waiting for the products of this lead-zinc mine. The workers are represented in this delegation by the head of the Yukon Federation of Labour, ready and eager to go back to work, having done everything that could be expected of labour. But the Government and its protege, Dome Petroleum, which took over the mine only to close it, have yet to make a move.
This is not an ordinary delegation. It represents the White Pass and Yukon Railway, the Yukon Federation of Labour, the territorial member from that riding, the town of Faro by its mayor, the Canadian Labour Congress, and other concerned citizens. From all over Canada groups have presented submissions, petitions, pleas and requests for action and in the face of the storming of the bastille-the Government's indifference-we have had an example of absolutely monumental inertia.

1 have mentioned the jobs that have been lost. This is something that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) do not like to hear. It interrupts the even tenor of those plans and schemes which they continually juggle in the air-from schemes to extract oil from coal, to the latest Pitfield exercise in positive thinking, to the newest centralist intervention in the economy. They do not like to be reminded about the hard facts of life, such as the fact that they have frittered away half a million jobs for half a million Canadians since taking office. These are unpleasant facts and they do not like to be reminded of unpleasant facts. When you are riding around in a bullet-proof limousine and handing out $800 per diem jobs to your friends and possible successors, you do not like to be reminded of things that are unpleasant. But sadly, after the remake it was the same old face of Liberal inaction.
We had development programs and make-work programs and new initiatives, announced with all the fanfare of a Government which spends more energy on announcing its putative achievements than it does in carrying them out. Nothing worked. The economy at this moment is being compared to the darkest days of the Depression. Does that dampen the spirits of Members opposite? Not a whit.
The Prime Minister flits to the Caribbean and promises that Canada will grant aid to governments that follow Marxist policies as well as those that choose democracy. That is
Income Tax
statesmanship all right. This lets our friends and allies know where Canada stands.
After three years of the worst Government in the history of this country, Canadians are borne down by a sense of oppression and gloom. They sense dark clouds of disaster folding over a nation that by every standard should enjoy the brightest and most positive progress of any nation in the world. We stand twenty-fourth, at the bottom of the heap-and the Government put us there.
People sense an abdication of leadership, a fear of the future, an uncertainty about on-going prospects. Canadians have an uneasy awareness of a Government that does not care, a Government in isolation, a Government that worries more about permitting its friends to make a living out of the taxpayer-as the Prime Minister said the other day of his friend in Toronto-than in producing good management for the majority of Canadians.
One has the distinct impression in speaking in this House, Mr. Speaker, that the Government is not listening. Member after Member rises, points out the defects in the Government's proposals, and then the trained seals rise in their places, the measure is approved and another fragment of our freedoms is lost.
This is another of those rag-tag, grab-bag Bills which this most incompetent of Governments has brought before this House. This Bill is the relic and remnant of one former Minister and the present Minister. It took two Ministers to get this mess together. The first has gone to his reward in External Affairs. His own changes to this budget would have brought about the resignation of any self-respecting Minister of Finance. The second is still with us, but he should not be after the disclosures of the last several days.
The legislation which we are now facing is a compendium of no less than three budgets. The first was introduced in November of 1981, the second follow-up budget in June of 1982, and the third by the present Minister in October of 1982. None of these budgets went through the House because of the Government's intense preoccupation with buying gas stations, imposing metric conversion on Canadians, cooking up Canagrex, operating its several hundred Crown corporations, and daydreaming about establishing more, totally outside the purview of Parliament. This Government can hardly bring itself together about such mundane things as budgetary measures or unemployment. This Government can hardly bring itself to bother about standard practices of an annual session of Parliament, with a Throne Speech once a year, with a budget once a year, with order and planning to assist in discharging the business of the country. Sir, you cannot operate a country that way; certainly you cannot operate a House of Commons that way. It cannot be done. Parliament is entitled to have budgets delivered and presented at regular intervals, consistent with the fiscal periods in which they apply.

Hear, hear!

Instead of that, we are not only asked to deal with budgets representing several past fiscal periods and budgetary measures inextricably intermingled one with the other, but now we are establishing the practice of projecting budgetary requirements into fiscal years not even yet upon us, with no explanation as to how funds will be spent for future requirements. Under the circumstances it is impossible to attempt to deal logically and coherently with matters before the House affecting the livelihoods of thousands upon thousands of Canadians.
In the middle of this frightful disarray the Government comes into the House with a demand for cash requirements for the next fiscal year but with no accompanying budgetary measures or budget at all. This is a further indication of the extent to which the Government has gone totally out of control. Not only can Government Members not enunciate clear and workable policies, not only have they failed to deal with the problems of unemployment and economic disarray, they cannot even look after such elementary housekeeping duties as bringing down budgets at proper times.
Parliament is now confronted with bits and pieces of three budgets, along with a demand for authority to borrow $14 billion, this being the cash requirement for a fourth budget which we have not even seen yet. That is not financial policy; that is total disarray. How can Canadians expect equitable and reasonable tax treatment from a Government which does not know where its next budget is coming from or where its last budget has gone? How can business or industry have confidence in a Government whose national accounts not only will not balance, they cannot even be found? Never has Parliament in my experience been confronted with such a situation.
Here is a session which has been creaking and groaning along for over three years, the longest single session in Canadian Parliamentary history, simply because the Government has neither the wit nor the intelligence to put together a Throne Speech to tell us what it intends to do. The reason is simple: they are the last to know.
No area of Canada has been harder hit by the incompetence of this Government than the area which I have the honour to represent. The people in Yukon are like the people in any other part of Canada. They like to pay their bills and they like to bring up their families with a modicum of security and stability, yet under the policies of the Government that security and stability have disappeared. When I hear the tragic figures of unemployment in the Atlantic Provinces, when I hear the tribulations which confront the forest and other industries in British Columbia and their tragic unemployment figures, Members will excuse me for suggesting that they might gasp a little if I tell them that the unemployment figures in Yukon are 30 per cent and higher. We have witnessed there the closing of our entire mining industry; every single mine in Yukon has been closed. Employment and investment have dried up entirely. We have felt the heavy hand of Government in an area in which the authorities in Ottawa neither understand nor show any great interest.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I thought the Tories believed in that.

I will convey that very interesting interjection to my constituents of Yukon. That interjection is typical of the hard-hided, uncaring, insensitive attitude typical of the Government across the way. We have suffered a mass exodus from Yukon as jobs have dried up and as incomes have disappeared.
Members of the House know that people pay extra premiums in oil, gas and electricity, extra premiums in food, clothing, medical care, as well as in transportation and shipping, yet we have had notice that the Government will begin now taxing northern benefits accorded to those people who have chosen to live and work in the North. Benefits which have been free from tax for well over 30 years are now being fallen upon by this insatiable, greedy Government, adding one more nail in the lid of the coffin of northern development.
When the former Conservative Government was in office- and I go back to 1957-there was meaning to the northern vision, there was meaning to northern development. It was a vision that was lit by the Conservative Government of the day in the minds of Canadians who suddenly became aware that 40 per cent of the nation lay above the sixtieth parallel, rich in resources. Programs were brought into play to provide the kind of incentive for people to populate that area of Canada and to bring about a realization of the richness of those resources for the benefit of all Canadians. That policy was carried on in the short seven months of the administration of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), but this Government is doing everything in its power not to encourage people to live in northern Canada but, rather, to totally discourage them. Indeed, there is that mentality among some who would like to create that part of Canada as a huge national park and leave it unsullied.
The budgetary measures in this Bill represent a continuing saga in Liberal incompetence and in Liberal unconcern. They brought in the first budget of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) in November, 1981. It was an exercise in futility. The Minister built castles in the air, and they have all come tumbling down. His budget was so remote and so divorced from reality that it sounded like one of the speeches of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), those he very rarely delivers in the House of Commons. I believe, in the 15 years he has been Prime Minister, that he has spoken some six times in the debates in the House of Commons. He considers this place a nuisance. He considers all of us nobodies when we are 40 feet off the Hill. In December they tried to put MacEachen's Humpty-Dumpty back together again, back on the wall, and they failed. In June they tried again, practically returning to the status quo. In October the substitute Minister of Finance brought in a new budget-he did not call it that-wiping out the efforts of his predecessor and providing the most emphatic vote of non-confidence in history from one Minister to another in the same Government.
March 1, 1983

What must concern Parliament and all who are committed to this institution is the cavalier disregard by the Government of the rights and privileges of Members. Surely we have a right to expect to have spelled out a coherent financial policy, carefully set forth in budgetary terms so that Parliament and Canadians will know where we are going. We have not had that. They do not care over there. They do not even participate in the debate on this important measure before us. We have had academic exercises, epistemological experiments, casually arrived at, flung before Parliament almost contemptuously sometimes weeks and months out of date, while the Government goes about its business of pillaging, yes, Sir, pillaging, the Treasury of this nation.
What is also disturbing is that while the House is faced with the detritus of three budgets, the wreckage of fiscal and monetary experimentation, there remains enough of the underlying philosophy to cause grave disquiet. The first MacEachen budget was an exercise in unwarranted, unjustified confiscation. It was based on the premise, clearly spelled out, that all income was the property of the Government to do with as it saw fit.
There has been nothing so approaching the divine right of kings since the demise of Charles I. The philosophy enunciated in that budget would find ready acceptance in any totalitarian dictatorship in the world. In fact, the Prime Minister himself, basking in the sunny breezes of St. Lucia two weekends ago, said that, as for him, he could see no difference between states with Marxist governments and those embracing democracy. Those are not my words, they are his.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They are not his at all.

The Parliamentary Secretary says I am misquoting the Prime Minister. Pray correct me. Let him tell me and Members of the House, Mr. Speaker, in what respect my quote of the Prime Minister's in St. Lucia is incorrect. I challenge him right now. The Parliamentary Secretary does not do so because he knows, Sir, that I quote the Prime Minister correctly. This is something we in the House have been aware of for a long time.
The Prime Minister has to be the focal point of the dry rot in this institution. He and his Government have contributed coldly and deliberately to the deterioration of Parliament by neglecting our procedures, by ignoring our traditions, by undermining the great principles of free expression and free debate, and by treating this institution as an afterthought, as did the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) just today by his refusal to say in the House what he ran to a press conference to say. When you undermine Parliament, Sir, you are striking at the freedom of all Canadians.
We have before us a series of tax measures, some of them contradictory, some of them mutually exclusive, all of them incoherent, disorganized, chronologically out of sync, leftovers, bits and pieces of three or four budgets. How does the Prime Minister and his Government expect Parliament to deal intelligently with what is nothing more than a fiscal dog's
Income Tax
breakfast? This kind of contemptuous disregard for the House of Commons permeates everything that is done on the other side of the House. While the Government asks this House, which has been sitting, as I have said, longer than any session in our history, for approval of this incredible melange of tax measures, most of which have been overtaken by economic shifts and changes, it goes on ladling out goodies to its friends and former colleagues. Here is a total disregard for what Parliament may think or do.
Former Ministers of this Government, with the ink scarcely dry on their discharge papers, are out making up packages with their friends in business, getting those packages approval at the departmental level by their former employees, and then getting approval by their friends in the Cabinet. In each case, they stand to make profits which would provide the ordinary Canadian with a worry-free retirement program for the rest of his or her life. The Prime Minister has produced a new guideline which he does not talk about. He does not want to talk about it. Perhaps it is between the lines. It is called the "belly up to the trough guideline."
In view of the last two weeks, I have spent some time redrawing the guidelines, not as they should be, not on the basis of analysis of what is there, which is enough for any Minister acting in a proper fashion, but on the basis of what the Prime Minister and his Government are doing. It reads something like this:
Any former Minister may have unrestricted access to the goodies of his former Department, providing he obtains the approval of his former colleagues who are now Ministers not earlier than two years after leaving the Government. This does not prevent him from entering negotiations with his former Department immediately, nor does it prevent his using his insider knowledge and contacts to set up cosy little packages with friends in industry so as to become eligible for special treatment denied to other Canadians. This can result in quite considerable profits to those involved, as in the Banff townsite case and the coal liquefaction case. There is no problem in bypassing tiresome departmental regulations which are only there to freeze out the uninitiated, or members of the general public and do not apply to former Ministers. Best of all, the whole procedure is entirely within the guidelines. I promised I would not forget you. Bless you, Pierre.
Hear, hear!

I saw the Hon. Member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey) smiling a moment ago because he will recognize the validity of that guideline.
This is the unwritten guideline, so confidential that even Iona has not seen it. This is the perception in the eyes of the Canadian public. And it is this perception, along with the incredible sloppiness of the Government, that is undermining Parliament as an institution of the people of this country. This Government, with the greatest expenditures, with the greatest deficit, with the greatest incompetence in the history of this country, has shown its absolute and utter disdain for Parliament.
In the Coalgate affair-some call it the Lalonde affair, some call it the MacEachen affair and some call it the Gillespie affair-

I call it the Coalgate affair because it embraces everyone. Rather than admitting error and throwing themselves on the mercy of the House, they have resorted to bitter attacks on those who have dared to question the obviously sleazy activities in which they have been engaged. Day after day, the Prime Minister took refuge in clouds of evasion and obfuscation and, in his own words, misleading statements to the House of Commons. The truth has slowly risen to the surface.
This trail has always led in the same direction-to Gillespie. There were side turns and side branches, carefully hidden in the underbrush, put together by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and his friends. One trail led to the Deputy Prime Minister, who was the Minister of Finance at the time and who also at the time was Vice-President of the Treasury Board, to whom went a couple of submissions concerning this matter. Presumably he acted in his capacity as Deputy Prime Minister and Minister responsible for Nova Scotia. Now he refuses to answer questions, ignores questions or just simply fails to appear. It appears that although he is still Deputy Prime Minister, he cannot, as Minister of External Affairs, give the House an accounting of what he did when he was Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Let's get back to the Income Tax Act.

The Parliamentary Secretary asks me what this has to do with the Income Tax Act. This Act asks us to tax Canadians so that the Parliamentary Secretary and the friends in his Party, led by those Ministers, can dole out favours, having a potential of $750,000 in profit in Canadian taxpayers' money, or an up front investment of $25,000 by Gillespie which he had already retrieved in the first year of the transaction. I trust that I have clarified, even for his thick skull, what this matter has to do with taxing Canadians. The Minister of External Affairs cannot give that accounting even though he was then, as now, Deputy Prime Minister.
One begins to see the reason for the sudden and bewildering Cabinet shuffle which took place a few months ago, which I described on that occasion as a shuffling of pallbearers, when the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources were suddenly shuffled to new roles which made it impossible under our rules to question either of them.
It is noteworthy that the present Minister of Finance has accepted his responsibility in this matter. He has made an explanation to the House. I, for one, cannot accept that explanation. I, for one, believe that despite the question of right or wrong, good or evil, he had an obligation under the traditions of this institution to tender his resignation. That he did not do. That obligation, because of the implication of the Deputy Prime Minister, was also upon him, an obligation which he has failed to fulfil. Loquacious enough on other occasions, the Deputy Prime Minister has preserved, in regard to the Gillespie affair, the attitude of Buddha personified. But
then, that is his common attitude whenever he or his Government is in difficulty. We sometimes wonder whether he is contemplating his navel or is lost in meditation, but he has shown no sign of following the lead, as shallow as it might be, of the Minister of Finance in making a clean breast of his participation in this whole shoddy affair. His attitude of noninvolvement is in stark contrast to the position he took in announcing the project when he was front and centre on the platform at Port Hawkesbury with dear Alastair.
If we were not aware of the purity of his intentions, the unblemished devotion shown in his record, it would appear that his present posture is one of a person burdened with guilt. It appears that he is satisfied to sulk in his tent, or his seat, and allow his colleague, the Minister of Finance, to bear the brunt of public inquiry into these activities. When searching for a reason for that kind of conduct on his part, one does not have to look far when one sees how the present Minister of Finance totally destroyed the credibility of the Minister for External Affairs when he was Minister of Finance in the presentation of that financial statement or budget.
I suggest that that is not the kind of attitude that would endear the Deputy Prime Minister to his colleagues on the front benches.
One has the feeling that if he chose, in his capacity as Deputy Prime Minister which was the capacity in which he acted at the time, he could elucidate many of the troubling issues in the Gillespie affair. Surely the Prime Minister must see that the time has come for the Deputy Prime Minister to break his silence and take the nation and the House into his confidence, as he once took Alastair Gillespie into his confidence. It is he who holds the key to unriddling the conundrum.
By speaking, he can get the Minister of Finance, who has been carrying the can for him, off the hook. He can relieve the Prime Minister of the burden of public criticism which he has been bearing on behalf of the Deputy Prime Minister. He can let the House and the public in on all the little secrets of this matter in an exercise which cannot be but of immense therapeutic value to himself.
Perhaps he could tell us what took place. Who inserted the funds for the synfuels program in the budget under the National Energy Program? It appears that the Deputy Prime Minister's original budget was more artful than it seemed. Perhaps he can elucidate what was in the submission that went to the Treasury Board and which bore the warning of Alastair Gillespie's involvement? He was, after all, Vice-President of the Treasury Board. He was both the Minister of Finance responsible for the budget and, of course, not just a member of the Treasury Board but Vice-President of the Treasury Board. Perhaps he might even go into the methods of persuasion that were used to screw the courage of the Minister of Energy at the time to the sticking point, after he became reluctant to sign the submission.
Everywhere one turns in this affair, one finds evidence of the fine hand of the Deputy Prime Minister.

March 1, 1983

Again, the Parliamentary Secretary does not really understand the rules of relevance. Yes, I say to him, this is the Income Tax Act. This Government is asking for taxes from the Canadian people so that it can pay off its friends, such as Macdonald, $925 a day, and give lucrative architectural jobs to close friends of the Prime Minister, such as Mr. Erickson, to build an embassy. There is a whole list of them which appeared in the newspaper the other day. 1 am surprised that the Parliamentary Secretary has not read of them.
The Deputy Prime Minister owes it to himself, to the country and to his Prime Minister to speak.
Therefore, we are brought to today when, under a spurious point of order, the Minister of Finance rises in his place to make yet another correction to his previous statements. He sat there for a week. Even accepting the fact that after the week end's search he knew on February 21 that he had prior knowledge, it was his responsibility then to take half a dozen steps to the Deputy Prime Minister to inform the House immediately that the misleading statements of the Prime Minister were no longer valid. He could have lifted the telephone to do that, it is amazing that all of a sudden Alexander Graham Bell and the technology that he brought to our commerce in this country and to our private discussions went out of style. Ministers started writing letters instead of lifting telephones. The Minister had an obligation to inform us immediately. He did not do that.
1 want to say a word or two before sitting down. 1 have touched on the taxation of northern benefits, and now I want to discuss another Cabinet document which came to my attention a short while ago.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It relates to the Income Tax Act, I guess.

It was sponsored by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) and relates to amending the Northern Inland Waters Act to make certain regulations which, in effect, would entirely lay to rest the Yukon placer mining industry. The Government has killed, has utterly destroyed, the hard rock mining industry in the Yukon, and now it is about to do the same to the placer mining industry. It will not get away with its intended amendments to the Northern Inland Waters Act. It will not get away with its intention to amend or completely revise the Yukon Placer Mining Act, because we intend to fight that kind of change every step of the way.
However, consider the Government's approach. We hear the Liberals self-righteously rising and saying, "We will abide by the spirit of the Freedom of Information Act. We will tell Members of Parliament more about Government business. We will inform Canadians more about what we do in Government on their behalf'.
I will read from a Cabinet document under the sponsorship of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development concerning amendments to the Northern Inland Waters Act.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council

"It is not intended"-the Parliamentary Secretary has interjected. I said in my remarks a few moments ago that the Liberals neither understood nor wished to understand northern Canada. The Parliamentary Secretary obviously does not. I am referring to an industry which produces 93 per cent of Canada's placer gold, and the Government's decision with respect to hearings which are now under way in Whitehorse will cost that industry in Yukon $270 million.

In keeping with the new bold spirit of the Government in making all this information accessible to Members of Parliament, let me quote from its own Cabinet document, sponsored by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, which states, "It is not intended to publicly announce the decision to amend the Act or to convene public meetings to explain the amendments or to obtain reaction and comments". That is the Government's approach.

speakerposition: Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: That's dictatorship.

It does things in secret, never letting it see the light of day because it might get some good ideas from Members of Parliament as well as public organizations which might like to have some input. This is the Government's idea of participatory democracy. That is why the Government can kiss goodbye any hopes of amending the Northern Inland Waters Act. That is why it can kiss goodbye any attempt to amend the Yukon Placer Mining Act without consultation with industry or with Yukoners, whom the Government has effectively frozen out of the public hearings which have been going on in the Yukon for the last two or three days. Industry is not even allowed input into those hearings which are top heavy with Ottawa bureaucrats and departmental Government figures comprising 70 per cent of those making submissions at the hearings.
I am sorry that I have not been able to convince the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Smith)-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: At least I have listened to you.

-that what I have been saying has any bearing on tax measures. I have failed to convince him because he does not want to understand, or he refuses to understand. He has a closed Liberal mentality. He has the mentality so common among all Liberals today. They think, "We sit here by divine right. This institution is ours. We are the only ones fit to govern the country. This should be a unitary state because there is no one else in the country who is competent to govern". With the example of the standard of the Government, particularly as demonstrated in the last two weeks, if Canadians accept the Liberal party's belief that it is the only one fit to

govern the country, all I can say is, God help my country. 1 will not believe it. We on this side do not accept it. At the first opportunity we will see those rascals out of the Government so that a fresh new breed can sweep into these halls and govern the country.

Mr. Speaker, it is often said that the sins of yesterday are the taxes of today, and that has probably never been more true than it is now. We have before us a document which is 295 pages long, producing for us the results of three budgets. It tells us that Canadians were deceived once again in the last election when they were told that all they must do is to vote Liberal and all their problems will be solved. They were promised cheap energy, cheaper taxes, a universal system of social welfare and total protection from the ravages of inflation and unemployment. All these promises were given by the Liberals to an innocent public.
The question arises, what is the Government's tax philosophy? What has happened to these principles of equity and fairness which we have the right to expect would be embraced in the tax policy of the Government? No one denies the Government the right to use the Income Tax Act as a leverage to regulate, to stimulate and to slow down an overheated economy. However, the Government has managed to produce a tax system which has very extended leverage to it, one which was designed to pursue certain, now clearly identifiable, ideological goals, these goals being total central control and total control of an economy. It is a system which extends leverage to those who are on the inside and which rewards political friends.
What happens to all the principles of equity and fairness? As soon as they were tabled, I reviewed the proposed changes to the Income Tax Act. I did not see anything which would relieve the plight of the truckers from my constituency who write to me. People who travel in that manner are away from home for two or three weeks at a time, travelling up the Alaska Highway. The Income Tax Act and the regulations allowed them to deduct $ 18 a day while away from home for income tax purposes. If Your Honour has ever travelled up and down the Alaska Highway, or between here and Montreal, or travelled anywhere in Canada, you know that you cannot live on S18 a day when you are away from home. Donald Macdonald knows that. He needs a stipend of $800 a day in order to live, while a trucker who is away from home on his job is allowed a sustenance deduction of only $18 a day.
It is not necessary to cite such a dramatic comparison, and no trucker travelling up the Alaska Highway wants to compare himself with Donald Macdonald. However, how about considering the bureaucrat who is dispatched from Ottawa to Kingston or to any place else? He is allowed a per diem of $28 for food, but not the trucker. I looked through these 294 pages and I found no relief in there for the trucker. There is no fairness or equity of any kind.
What has happened to the principle of the ability to pay? What has happened to a tax Act based on principles of equity,
fairness and the redistribution of wealth, as well as the ability to pay, meaning that you pay a higher rate of tax if you are able?
My Leader just told you about some of the discrepancies that exist in the tax Act as it applies to northern residents. The ability of Canadians to pay taxes differs very dramatically in accordance with where one lives. When you have to pay up to $5 per gallon of gasoline, $400 per month to heat your home, and up to 2.5 times the southern rate for essential food for your family, as do people in the North, your ability to pay tax is less, obviously, than the ability of those who live in Toronto, Montreal or Ottawa. Is that fact respected in this tax Bill? The only reference to it is that northern benefits, which we have allowed northern steelworkers and workers in larger companies with the protection of large unions, are to be phased out over a three-year period. These people have traditionally received northern benefits for housing and for trips outside to civilization. We are now told in this 294-page document that those benefits are to be phased out. Does it contain anything to replace those benefits? There is nothing there. It does not respect the principles of equity, fairness and the ability to pay.
What has happened to the principle of the ability to comprehend? Has the Government made an effort to make this tax Act understandable to the average Canadian? Should I read to you, as some of my colleagues have done, some of the paragraphs in this tax Act that are convoluted and totally incomprehensible?
These people in Government do not do anything without a reason. The reason this Bill is so complicated and convoluted is that it is based not on the principles of the ability to pay, comprehend, or equity and fairness, but rather on the mushroom principle which goes something like this: keep people in the dark and cover them with horse manure, and you can do anything you like. That is the principle on which this document is based.
I could not pretend, and I suggest you could not either, to understand fully our tax Act today. There is a whole new cult of bureaucrats, corporate and tax lawyers. One used to be able to fill out one's own tax form. When it got a little more complicated and you had a little income and wanted to deduct money you sent overseas to help your ailing mother or relatives in a distressed country from which you had come, you could go to a tax accountant in April and ask him to help you make out your income tax return. That is not the case any longer. If you want to take advantage of all the things written into this Act today and you do not want to be shafted, you have to hire a tax lawyer. At one time you used to have a family doctor. Now you need a family tax lawyer.
It is also suggested that the crime of taxation is not in the taking but in the way it is being spent. This Government tells us that the reason it has to come to us for $5 billion in additional borrowing authority, and the reason our tax bill is increasing, as Government spending is increasing this year, by
March 1, 1983

17 per cent while everyone else's income increases are limited by the six and five program, is that the locked in social programs to which the Government is committed are growing. Naturally when the economy is in a decline the demand placed on these social programs increases. That is a reasonable argument.
This tax Bill also indicates that measures which have been laid before this House have put a cap on the social program. No longer are Family Allowances indexed to the rate of inflation. No longer are old age pensions indexed to the rate of inflation. The Government has protected itself against any unreasonable increases in the demand on our social contracts and programs.
Let me tell you something and make a comparison. It has been estimated that it would cost this country $2 billion to put in place an actuarially sound pension program that would compare with the best in the world, such as that of Sweden and West Germany. In that way when a worker had completed his productive years he would have 80 per cent of his earned wages as a pension. It is estimated that that would cost this country $2 billion. Imagine that.
This Government spent $6 billion buying service stations throughout the country to put in place a National Energy Program which has invited the scorn of everyone, and created a reputation that we will not live down in the next 25 years. That expenditure has not created one new job or found one new barrel of oil. It has done nothing. The Government spent $6 billion, three times what it would cost to put a universal program in place, to secure totally the future of every person who has ever made a contribution to the work base of this country. That is why I say the crime of taxation is not in the taking but in the way it is being spent.
What this Government is doing is to tax the poor. It has capped Family Allowances and old age pensions and it is phasing out the northern benefits. It has not forgotten to reward its friends. Mr. Gillespie will have no problem in coming to grips with the hardships of the times. The Liberals over there know how to reward their friends. Of the 24 million people in this country only a small number are Liberal friends, and that circle is getting smaller and smaller as the just society is becoming more and more just for Liberals.

speechtext:
It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 45, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: The Hon. Member for South West Nova (Miss Campbell)- Fisheries-Allocation of non-surplus stock to European
