Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly)-Energy-Request that oil price be allowed to drop, (b) Price of gasoline.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-139, to amend the Statute law relating to Income Tax (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker, of all the Bills which have come before Parliament during the present session of Parliament, Bill C-139 ranks as one of the most complicated. The bulky Bill to amend the statute law relating to income tax, as previous speakers have mentioned, is some 294 pages in length. Yet our Minister of Finance is asking the House to whip it through because he feels the various tax consultants need this legislation so they can fulfil their obligations to Canadians, and it will delay the return of income tax refunds to taxpayers if it is held up here.
The Minister is particularly justified in asking for a decision on this tax Bill. The tax laws have been so muddied by the process of budgets within recent years and subsequent financial statements which amend this and disallow that, that few Canadians, even tax experts, can claim to understand the income tax laws thoroughly. In that sense this Bill is required to clear the air.
Parliamentarians who have been debating this Bill are deeply concerned because it is too difficult to understand; it is simply too cumbersome a document to be swallowed in one bite. The risk connected with this Bill is that out of frustration, while under the pressure of time limitation on debate, Bill C-139 will get the green light from the House without Members being sure of exactly what is in the legislation. The Government's staff required some 389 days to draft this document. It embraces changes in income tax law introduced in budgets, and budgetary statements issued in November and December of 1981, the June budget of 1982, and the October, 1982, financial statement. It represents the work of two Finance Ministers. We need to have a better schedule of producing and debating these Bills. We need to further expand the parliamentary reform that has been established. We are still considering measures that were introduced in budgetary documents in excess of 15 months ago.

March 1, 1983
Income Tax
As previous speakers have indicated in this debate, I too would ask why the wording in this legislation has to be so complicated. The Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) and a number of other Members have indicated their concern. I would ask the House to consider this passage referring to taxation to cover an employee being issued a company car. If, Mr. Speaker, you can make sense out of it, you will do a lot better than I. The legislation indicates, and I quote:
An amount that is a reasonable standby charge for the automobile for the aggregate number of days in a taxation year during which it was made available by an employer or by a person related to an employer shall be deemed to be the amount equal to the product obtained when
(a) where the employer or the person related to the employer owned the automobile at any time in the year, an amount in respect of its cost to the employer equal to the percentage thereof obtained when two per cent is multiplied by
the quotient obtained when such of the aggregate number of days hereinbefore referred to as were days during which the employer or the person related to the employer owned the automobile is divided by 30 (except that if the quotient so obtained is not a full number, and exceeds one, it shall be taken to the nearest full number or, if there is no full number, then to the full number next below-
I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether you or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) would be kind enough to explain that phraseology to us. Many individuals are making a great deal of money interpreting tax laws. As the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) indicated earlier, at one time we could fill out our own tax returns, but with complicated legislation such as this, it is impossible.
We oppose the limitation of the indexation factor on personal taxes according to the six and five program. This is nothing more than a sneaky income tax increase. If the Government wishes to increase taxes, let it do so. To slip this through without proper debate and backed up by a massive advertising program supporting the six and five program is pure and simple deceit.
Now is not the time for us as Parliamentarians to increase taxes. The economy is still in decline. Canadians should be encouraged to spend their money. A tax increase to feed the ever-growing appetite of the Government is counter-productive.
If the Government feels so strongly about the size of the deficit, let it cut its own spending. Let it curtail the 50 per cent increase in ministerial travel. Let it cut back on the size of the increase in the Minister's Department, and show it means business. Let it cut back where any businessman would start- on overhead and the administrative costs of running the Government. We have yet to hear why the overhead costs in the 12 largest Departments of this Government will increase by 17.1 per cent. As previous speakers have indicated, what we need is a new tax act, something to which everyday-Canadians can relate and which they can understand. It should be simplified so that tax rules are easily understood. I rather doubt that this will come about with the present administration. Their preoccupation is with the distribution rather than the generation of wealth in this country. They have stifled the growth of every sector in this country.
I wish to share with Hon. Members an article which appeared in The Edmonton Journal relating to farm bankruptcies in Canada. It reads:
Bankruptcies continue to reap a grim harvest across rural Canada as another 33 farmers were forced out of business in January, the Consumer Affairs Department reported Monday.
The figure is 32 percent higher than in January 1982-
I have received, as I am sure all Members have, hundreds of letters relating to the budgetary measures and the legislation before us. Most of it is critical of what this Government is doing. Let me relate the one item on which we receive the most correspondence. It is with regard to the use of company automobiles. The Government did take a step back in this area and withdrew some of the provisions, but it did not go nearly far enough. I would ask the Minister of Finance to give further consideration to this area because this tax is totally unjustified.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to participate in this debate at this time. I am one of millions of Canadians who have come to the conclusion that after a number of budgets and economic statements and other activities of this Government, of the former Minister of Finance, now Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) and the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), as well as the changes, reversals and hesitations, we should get on with the job and pass something in the House of Commons after so much talk of uncertainty on the part of the Government.
I do not propose to speak at great length. I want to address one or two ideas at second reading stage. This may be of some assistance to the Government in terms of its future activities. In considering future taxation measures, we would like that element of certainty which Canadians require as to the amount of taxes they will be expected to pay. Also, we would like to know the time-frame within which these matters should be considered by Parliament.
When the budgets or economic statements of November, June and October were presented, I am sure Members on both sides of the House had roughly the same experience in their constituency offices. My office was deluged with delegations and representations from a wide spectrum of constituents in every type of occupation, farmers, small-business persons and those in the life insurance industry. God knows we heard from the life insurance industry and those who have life insurance policies. We heard from those who had certain investments which they hoped to use in order to support themselves during their retirement years.
They came into my office to see their Member of Parliament regarding the proposals put forward in the House of Commons. They sought advice as to what they should do in terms of their business and investment as a result of the proposals in the statements and budgets.
It was a preposterous and ridiculous situation. One gentleman who came to my office sought advice on a number of propositions set forth in the budget of the former Minister of Finance. He asked what the proposals meant. 1 could not tell
March 1, 1983

him, and 1 informed him that I could get no clarification either from the Minister on the floor of the House of Commons. I recommended that he ask an accountant what he should do. He said, "I am an accountant". That is the situation in which we find ourselves. Canadians, regardless of their profession, have no idea as to what the Government has in mind.
We cannot get answers from the Government. There is confusion. Business decisions are held up. The Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) and the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Campbell) know this. They receive as many calls from their constituents as I do asking what this proposal means and how to plan their business.
1 wish to relate to the House some of the information which those of us on the Special Committee on Procedure were privy to and were able to obtain on a recent visit to Westminster. We had the opportunity of examining the whole question of accountability and the way in which the United Kingdom, the Parliament of that country, deals with matters such as amendments to the Income Tax Act or taxation matters generally. In that country, Mr. Speaker, the question was raised some years ago as to whether or not taxation measures, once they were introduced in the budget, were effective before the Ways and Means motions and the legislation specifying the exact changes to the Income Tax Act or other legislation of the United Kingdom was passed. That is the same situation which we have now. The question has been raised on different occasions by Hon. Members of the Opposition as to whether or not the people of Canada are expected to pay these taxes which are brought down in the budgets even though we have not yet passed the legislation formally putting into effect the provisions set forth in the budgets.
The matter came to a point of confrontation in the United Kingdom in about 1923. It was challenged by a Member of Parliament there. The matter was to go to the courts for adjudication as to whether or not these taxation measures referred to in budgets were effective as of the date of the budget and were to be applied immediately notwithstanding the fact that Parliament had not yet spoken on these provisions. The resolution on the part of the Parliament of the United Kingdom was to pass an Act which provides for dealing with taxation measures brought down by a budget. And what they do in that country-and maybe it is something we should be looking at in this country as well-is to specify by statute that taxes which are brought into effect by a budget statement become effective on the date specified in the budget. They remain in effect for a certain period of time, within which time it is anticipated that the actual Ways and Means motions, and the amendments to the legislation in question, must be brought before the House and voted upon.
I mention this experience in Britain because of what I believe we have seen over the course of the last two and a half years in terms of the people of Canada, their great confusion and concern over exactly where they stand with respect to the different provisions set forth in the budget, because they were asked to pay taxes which were to be deducted at source with respect to certain benefits, and yet the amendments were not
Income Tax
brought down and passed for various reasons, including indecision on the part of the Government.
We have this unfortunate experience, therefore, Mr. Speaker, which has really, I believe, brought home to us a substantial lesson, that sometimes, even though we may object to a particular tax A, B or C, it is more important to have certainty as to what the changes are going to be than to be concerned about the merits of the actual tax provision itself. The reason is that the damage which is caused to the lives of individual Canadians, to the business sector, the effect it has on our total economy, is owing to the indecision which exists in the minds of the people when investment decisions are held back because of the fact that the Government does not know what it wants to do, or is not certain.
Delays in bringing in its legislation, amendments to the Income Tax Act, cause serious problems, and the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) would fully understand that since he has taken over his portfolio. This situation probably has been one of his greatest preoccupations as he receives complaints from Canadians and questions as to what they can expect in terms of actual amendments, when they can expect the amendments to be passed, and when the Government is going to make a decision about which ones they will keep and which ones they will drop from the budget. He knows the consequences this has had on investment in our country.
I simply say, therefore, by way of general advice to the Government and to Members of Parliament, that perhaps the time has come for us to look at some rules governing the time in which these budgetary provisions have to be dealt with by the House of Commons. There should be some opportunity for Members of Parliament to raise legitimate concerns or make constructive suggestions with respect to the advisability of these measures, but in due course it seems to me that what we have to do is to let the people of Canada know, as Parliamentarians in the House of Commons, where they are going so that they can make decisions about business investments, and when they will have the official decision with respect to budgetary matters.
I share that concern of many Canadians who have written to me. This Government has given me and all Members of Parliament more work in responding to letters of complaint and letters of clarification than any other Government that I can remember. That is saying something, because I have received a lot of letters of complaint with respect to the activities and policies of this Government. This budget has brought me more correspondence than any other single matter because of the way in which this Government has mishandled the matter. Unlike the Minister of State for Finance, I do not have a signature machine in my office. I have to sign all those letters, as well as compose and dictate them. I have to speak to my constituents. 1 do not have a phalanx of executive assistants to protect me as the Minister has protecting him from his constituents. I have to speak to my constituents, and 1 am proud and pleased to be able to do so. I do not look for that

kind of work. 1 try to be constructive and give the Government the benefit of constructive advice, and that is the policy I bring to Government.
Now I say to the Minister that 1 hope he has learned his lesson in his new responsibility and that he will take my suggestion to his colleagues and bring something before Parliament which would allow us to deal with these matters on a more rational basis.

subtopic: FISHERIES-ALLOCATION OF NON-SURPLUS STOCK TO EUROPEAN ECONOMIC COMMUNITY
FISHERIES-ALLOCATION OF NON-SURPLUS STOCK TO EUROPEAN ECONOMIC COMMUNITY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I realize that seven minutes is not much time in which to try to put down all my concerns about the question I raised on January 31, 1983. The question concerns the allocation of nonsurplus stocks by the Government for market accessibility in the marketplace. I should like to define the term "nonsurplus".

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: FISHERIES-ALLOCATION OF NON-SURPLUS STOCK TO EUROPEAN ECONOMIC COMMUNITY
speechtext: Order, please. The Hon. Member for South West Nova (Miss Campbell) has the floor.

subtopic: FISHERIES-ALLOCATION OF NON-SURPLUS STOCK TO EUROPEAN ECONOMIC COMMUNITY
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I do not know if Hansard got everything that has gone on, it has been so noisy.
It used to be that we talked about traditional and nontraditional stocks. Then we talked about under-utilized and utilized species. Now the Department of Fisheries and Oceans is using the term non-surplus and surplus. For the benefit of Hon. Members I shall explain that the allocation of nonsurplus fish stocks is the allocation of stocks that Canadians in the fishing industry can use. It has become the practice over the last year or so to allocate non-surplus stocks for market accessibility.
When I questioned the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane), he said he felt it was a perfectly suitable mechanism since the industry appeared to want it, and that we could allocate non-surplus stocks for market accessibility. This one related to the European Economic Community, last year it related to the Portuguese, and I understand that there will be another one shortly with the Portuguese as well that will double for them the amount of non-surplus stock in our fisheries this year.
I do not think it is a good practice for industry to suggest this, or for the Department of Fisheries and Oceans or the Department of External Affairs to go out and find new market accessibility by using non-surplus stocks.
1 would ask Hon. Members to recall the days prior to the 200-mile jurisdiction being declared by Canada. At that time, all of the industry-inshore and offshore fishermen, small and big companies-protested against foreigners being in our waters. With the advent of the 200-mile jurisdiction foreign fishing was eliminated, except when they were going after what we considered stocks surplus to our needs. They were given allocations of surplus stock within our waters. I stress "surplus" Mr. Speaker.
1 feel very strongly that to give up fish that we can use for market accessibility is not a good trading mechanism for the Government to be involved in.
Adjournment Debate
1 asked the question prior to the publication of the Kirby Report. I had already spoken to the Kirby Commission about this. 1 realized that one of the main objectives of the Kirby Task Force was that the Atlantic fishing industry should be economically viable on an on-going basis, viable implying an ability to survive downturns with only a normal business failure rate and without Government assistance.
It is very nice to have that type of objective. We find that the Government assistance that will be available as a result of the Kirby Report will be about $198 million. In 1974-75 when the fishing industry was also having problems it was $150 million. Yet the problem that Kirby recognized has not been corrected. On page 49 of his report he quoted from the 1928 Royal Commission on the Maritimes and Quebec Fisheries. I realize that my time is short, but 1 will read it quickly. It reads:
The demands of the consumer must continue to dictate-
This was taken from a 1928 report. It continues:
-the form in which fish are marketed. Consumption always regulates sales, and sales regulate not only production but the particular form of the product.
I say that it is the marketing end on which we are concentrating here. The report further indicated:
The declaration of the 200-mile limit in 1977 served to heighten interest in selling Canadian fish products.
He accepted that. The only disappointing thing was that he did not go further. He did not allow for the fact that what has gone wrong over the last number of years is that although the industry has gone out and established new markets in traditional stocks, there are also gluts in the catching of that fish which serve to depress established markets. Because of the depressed state of the markets, we had to find new and alternative means to find new markets. This brings me back to the point concerning the use of non-surplus stocks for access to markets.
I say that because it is the wrong form of marketing. The Kirby Report recommended close to $50 million for marketing over the next five years. That is not nearly enough money when we are dealing with a natural resource which is food for the world. Yet this recommendation was accepted. Also it was accepted that the Kirby Report recommended over-the-side sales and non-allocation of surplus stocks for new market accessibility, to go along with the $50 million for new markets.
How much more will we trade of a resource which should not be bartered that way? We should have an effective industry and the involvement of Governments, both provincial and federal, so that we can go out and use the capacity we have built up over the 200-mile limit rather than decrease the capacity because Kirby had said that we will do marketing in the old direction rather than going for a new type of marketing. Perhaps this means Governments and industry getting involved with a natural resource. 1 do not think this has been considered by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans when he allowed this non-surplus allocation or in the Kirby Report

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish I had at least equal time to answer the questions of the Hon. Member for South West Nova (Miss Campbell). She has raised, in an articulate manner, in a very emotional manner and in a manner to which we in the House have become accustomed, the needs and concerns of her constituents. She referred to many of the questions confronting the Atlantic fisheries. She has gone through the whole scope of very important questions in her seven minutes. I will try to address one or two of the main ones.
She talked about the EEC agreement which Canada signed, and her concern that we have not obtained a good deal. I want to tell her, on behalf of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) and the Government of Canada, that we are concerned that the EEC has not lived up to the spirit and intent of that agreement.
The deal, which was signed in 1981, provided for a number of areas of co-operation between Canada and the EEC, but primarily, from the Hon. Member's point of view and concern, it provided for the promotion of economic and commercial cooperation. From the Canadian perspective, the supplementary agreement was designed mainly to assist our exporters to diversify and expand sales of their product into Europe. Canada is the world's leading exporter of fish products in terms of value, but we concentrate almost exclusively on the United States market. It was thought that this was a way of breaking into European markets. This is a very important concern for the Government and for Canadian producers.
In order to achieve improved access to EEC markets for Canadian cod and herring products, the cost to Canada would be a limited amount of surplus and non-surplus fish to be caught by European vessels. Regrettably, during 1982, the first year of operation of the agreement, the EEC failed to fulfil its obligations with respect to market access. Canada, on the other hand, honoured its obligations fully in 1982.
Canadian Government representatives have, on a number of occasions, as has the Minister personally, informed the EEC authorities of our strong dissatisfaction with the operation of the long-term agreement. Both the Minister of Fisheries and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) have recently discussed the matter with senior EEC representatives.
My time is short. Let me say this. Disagreement will be interpreted by Canada in future in so far as it benefits the Europeans in direct relation to their commitment to live up to the spirit and the intent of the agreement that was signed, that is, to allow Canadian producers access to European markets. Perhaps my few words today will improve the situation.

On February 11,1 asked the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) a question that directly related to a practice of which the House became aware earlier in the week. That practice concerned the issuance of tax returns by the Department of National Revenue to individual taxpayers, changing the practice that had existed in the past. The return now discloses the income of the taxpayer for the immediately preceding taxation year together with the identified social insurance number of the spouse of the taxpayer. These returns in blank form for the 1982 taxation year had been dispatched by the Department of National Revenue to all taxpayers. They were mailed in the customary fashion enclosing information which had not previously appeared on blank forms. Canada Post Office, since that date, has indicated that approximately 10 per cent to 15 per cent of blank tax forms dispatched to individual taxpayers go astray.
Members of the House are very concerned about the consequences of the practice of including within blank form information that might be material to others. I asked the Minister, having regard to a statement which had been made by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. LeBIanc) as repeated to a reporter for The Toronto Star on February 7, and having regard to the comments he made in connection with the amount of rent that tenants should pay to landlords, whether there was not some indication that this practice of including information on blank tax returns might be part and parcel of an arrangement to see a plan which was approved by the Minister of Public Works put into play. If I may just quote from the article which appeared in The Toronto Star on February 7, 1983, it reads:
LeBIanc told The Star he would like to see all tenants pay at least 25 to 30 per cent of their before-tax income for accommodation. This way, he believes, rent controls could be eliminated.
"There are quite a lot of people who are living at quite a bit less than what has been deemed as the norm of 25 to 30 per cent of income for lodging. I think quite a bit less in some cases," he said-
My concern with the issue raised by the Minister is, of course, that the issue of the amount a landlord extracts from a tenant for rent is a matter of provincial rights. Under the Constitution, Section 92 of the British North America Act specifically designates as a power allocated to the Provinces, property and civil rights. Certainly in my Province of Ontario, and I suspect in all other Provinces in Canada, the provincial Government has taken advantage of this unquestioned right granted to provincial Governments and has enacted legislation under the Landlord and Tenant Act which deals with the right of landlords and tenants.
It is completely inappropriate and misguided on the part of the Minister of Public Works to intervene in a matter which is

Mr. Speaker, this question arose in the context of other questions regarding information printed on personalized tax returns which were recently mailed for the 1982 taxation year. At that time, the Hon. Member for North York (Mr. Gamble), for reasons which are difficult to fathom, chose to raise questions about rental payments as a percentage of a taxpayer's total income. He appeared to be concerned about the confidentiality of tax information and to be under the illusion that some arrangements had been made to disclose information about taxpayers' income so that it could be used as a basis for determining the appropriate rent for an individual. I do not know if that is a fair statement of his position, but it is all that one can gather from what he said at the time.
Let me assure him and all Hon. Members that the confidentiality provisions of the Income Tax Act remain in place and no amendment is contemplated which would go remotely along the lines that appear to disturb him. Basically, those confidentiality provisions require that information gathered for purposes of administering the Income Tax Act shall be used for that purpose only. Any exception is clearly spelled out in the Act, such as the one that permits the use of income tax information to develop tax policy, which is a perfectly reasonable idea, to be sure.
As the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) indicates, his colleague, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Adjournment Debate
LeBlanc), has expressed a view as to what he thought would be a reasonable share of an individual's income that could be spent on rent. This is a very common sociological concept and it is surprising that the Hon. Member would not be familiar with it. It is certainly a giant leap from these to a belief that there is some kind of plan to make income tax information available to landlords.

subtopic: ENERGY-REQUEST THAT OIL PRICE BE ALLOWED TO DROP. (B) PRICE OF GASOLINE
ENERGY-REQUEST THAT OIL PRICE BE ALLOWED TO DROP. (B) PRICE OF GASOLINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I wish to expand upon this evening relates to the question which was raised in the House today and on numerous other days about the price of crude oil in Canada. What is being questioned at the present time is the issue of an election promise and a commitment made by the federal Government to maintain the price of oil in Canada below the world price.
One of the quotations used from those promises is from the Prime Minister's statement on national television during the election campaign when he indicated that his Party was prepared to keep the price of oil below the world price and that it would not be set by OPEC nations. We find that promise in question today. The unfortunate part of it is that the Government, with its $89 billion in expenditures which it is facing, is in very difficult times. As well, there is an extremely large deficit this year. The fear in Canada is that instead of addressing the economy as a whole, the Government will address only the need for its own revenues as well as again narrowly concentrating on the energy sector. The major concern is that this Government live up to its election promises and commitments under the National Energy Program and allow the Canadian price to remain below the world price and to track downward as that world price moves. If that were to happen, we would find a very large improvement in the fortunes of farmers, fishermen, manufacturers and small businesses. In addition, we would find that Canadian goods were more competitive on the world markets. Beyond that, communities such as the ones I represent would be able to offset generously transportation costs and make general improvements in the quality of life of consumers.
The unfortunate other side of the coin is that if the Government opts to push Canadian prices up to or beyond the world price level, Canadian goods would become non-competitive. As has been predicted by a number of leading organizations and financial analysts, the Canadian economy would continue to recover more slowly than its trading partners. In addition, it would appear that the major and immediate beneficiaries of a move to push up the price of Canadian old oil, or old new oil, depending on how one classifies our present conventional reserves, would be a small number of multi-national oil companies. There would be no direct, beneficial effect on smaller Canadian companies dealing in the frontier areas, holding most of the new oil, which is at world price or higher, and it would certainly do nothing to alleviate the problems of those

March 1, 1983
Adjournment Debate
organizations which the Government strove to put in business under the National Energy Program.
Ultimately, the major problem facing us today is the fact that the National Energy Program, as devised in 1980, is in a state of collapse. There is no doubt that Canadianization has gone ahead, as the Minister correctly pointed out the other day. Nevertheless, in the present economic circumstances, those companies are in the greatest jeopardy, carrying as they do larger debt loads and dealing with areas of the country, especially Canada lands, where the costs of operation are extremely high. Therefore, those companies are in danger of losing their activities while, in fact, the major multinational corporations, the ones that we tried to deal with, are in a much stronger position in relation to Canadian companies.
The conservation effort has certainly moved ahead, and structural changes have occurred in the economy. However, on the other side of the coin, we are confronted with a severe cutback in the use of energy because of the recession, and the recession does not reflect the true need for appropriate sources of energy.
The next problem, of course, concerns Government revenues and the collapse of the National Energy Program. The federal Government moved ahead in an attempt to concentrate on one single industrial sector, which was probably the greatest single failing of the federal Government. It was a quick cash grab. We have seen the projected revenues drop from $65 billion down to approximately $30 billion, and continuing to drop to $20 billion. In fact, the projections for economic growth and for revenue sharing by the federal Government certainly depict a very difficult situation.
The National Energy Program as it related to economic growth between now and the end of the century was based exclusively on megaprojects which have all gone down the drain. Again, there has been a tremendous failing, not only of the national energy policy but also of our economic policy, or lack of one.
The question with which we are dealing is an integral part of the National Energy Program which has gone amok, and a made-in-Canada oil price is what we have basically considered, and it will have to be maintained. It is a fact that Canadians, if given a slightly beneficial price in relation to the world price of oil, would gain the advantage. There would be an acceleration in economic recovery which would improve the entire country.
The last aspect of the collapse of the National Energy Program which we are attempting to address tonight concerns the agreements between the producing and consuming Provinces. We are in a state of absolute turmoil. Recent events between the Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland have been of tremendous concern to the people of Canada and to the people of Newfoundland. The federal Government's role in that process has been less than honourable, I would suggest. Further, a wedge must not be driven between Alberta and Canada. It is very necessary to resolve the problems arising in an attempt to come to an agreement
with the Province of Newfoundland in a fair and equitable
way.
[DOT]	(1825)
I think that the sixth point is the necessity of reaching agreements that will develop a unity of purpose between the producing Province and the consuming Provinces, with representation from the federal Government, is vitally important, and the fact that it matters not whether the federal Government is able to exercise jurisdiction through the courts. Ultimately the caring and sharing and the fair approach of the National Energy Program which was outlined in that basic document is not being displayed or adhered to by the federal Government. What we see on the part of the federal Government, particularly in the Newfoundland agreement, is a failure to take into account the needs of certain regions in this country for some control over the pacing and nature of development that occurs there, within the greater context of energy security for Canada as a whole.

speakeroldname: Mr. Garnet M. Bloomfield (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: ENERGY-REQUEST THAT OIL PRICE BE ALLOWED TO DROP. (B) PRICE OF GASOLINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 18 months ago today an agreement was signed between the Government of Canada and the Province of Alberta which established the basis for our current petroleum pricing policy. This policy is that the world price is paid for oil imported into Canada and for newly discovered oil from domestic sources, while a maximum of 75 per cent of the world price is paid for oil produced in Canada that was discovered several years ago. The pricing mechanism administered by the government provides for a blending of these prices and, consequently, the Canadian price of petroleum products paid by consumers is always lower than the international price.
To encourage greater use of our abundant natural gas resources, our pricing policy includes a provision whereby the price of natural gas in the market is determined at Toronto in a 65 per cent price relationship with oil. The prices of oil and gas also strongly influence the prices of electrical energy and other energy sources and, consequently, our entire energy price structure is established at highly competitive levels in relation to energy prices in other countries.
[DOT]	(1830)
The Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) in this House on February 22 stated that the U.S. price of gasoline was only 95 cents a gallon whereas the price in Canada is $2 or more a gallon. Even if one makes the generous assumption that he was expressing the U.S. price in terms of the U.S. dollar and the American gallon, and comparing it with the Canadian price in imperial gallons, his apples and oranges comparison is still in error. The fact is that Canadian and U.S. gasoline prices are not greatly different on an average basis. Where Canadian gasoline prices do exceed those south of the border, it is largely due to higher provincial Government taxes in relation to state taxes in the U.S. Heating oil prices in Canada are considerably lower than U.S. heating
March 1, 1983

oil prices. It should be noted too, that our gasoline prices are very much lower than those in European countries.
As the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) noted in responding to the Hon. Member's question on February 22, the oil pricing policy has not been changed. Under agreements in operation since the latter part of 1981 with the Governments of Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, Canadians are benefiting from lower oil prices than if our prices were set at international levels.
Representations have been made by those who feel that changes are now needed in the 75 per cent relation to the international level and that the domestic price should be raised
Adjournment Debate
immediately, or in steps, to the international ceiling. The Government understands their views but would be extremely reluctant to change the basic policy. In any event, it would be premature at this time of great price uncertainty to take any final decisions. What can be said with certainty is that price and decisions for the future will have careful regard to the interests and concerns of producers and consumers, and to the objectives of regional and economic growth.
